Requirements and further information can be found here on the Honors in the Arts website.

rows.name: ARTS-MIN
rows.catalogDescription: Complement your undergraduate degree with a minor in Interdisciplinary Arts. You’ll deepen your overall understanding of the arts, familiarize yourself with the theory and techniques of arts, and develop a diverse set of skills to become a more sophisticated scholar and maker of arts.

customFields.A3i6E:
The Interdisciplinary Arts Minor (“Inter-Arts Minor”) allows students in any major to design a study plan that combines their critical and creative interests as they learn to make meaningful connections across multiple disciplines. Through a small set of core classes, electives, and a senior year capstone, students in the Inter-Arts Minor will learn theories and techniques of creative practice and research and become familiar with a wide array of art, from live performance to creative writing, visual art to multimedia installation, and much in between.

Students interested in pursuing a Minor in Interdisciplinary Arts should contact Associate Director Jessi Pipert (jpipert@stanford.edu) for more information and to begin the planning process.

Inter-Arts Minor and Honors in the Arts

Any student in the Minor in Interdisciplinary Arts who is interested in creating a senior honors thesis is encouraged to apply for Honors in the Arts in their junior year. Honors in the Arts students are required to develop a symposium presentation in addition to their creative research project. Learn more about Honors in the Arts here.

Honors in the Arts is an application-based program.

See Interdisciplinary Arts Minor for more details.

requisitesSimple.name: Narrative Text
requisitesSimple.notes:
To earn a Minor in Interdisciplinary Arts, students must complete at least 27 units of coursework in the program and a senior capstone project. Required coursework includes a foundational class in interdisciplinary methods, an experiential arts course, and 13-15 units of electives that focus on the intersection of two or more disciplines. The minor culminates in an interdisciplinary capstone over the senior year and is supported by a faculty advisor and an accompanying series of workshops.

All core and elective courses should be completed prior to commencing the capstone sequence (ARTSINST 200A, B and C) in senior year. Petitions to complete some elective and/or core courses concurrently with the senior workshop sequence may be approved if the study plan presents adequately robust preparation. However, no minor requirements may be completed after the workshop sequence (e.g. during a co-term year after completion of the workshop sequence).

Students must declare the minor in Axess no later than the Final Study List Deadline of the autumn quarter of their senior year, although they are encouraged to declare sooner. Students are invited to discuss the minor with the Stanford Arts Institute’s Associate Director and prepare a Plan of Study that includes the focus of the minor study and a list of elective courses planned to fulfill the requirements. Students must also complete a Capstone Proposal in the spring quarter of their junior year. The Faculty Director must approve the Study Plan and Capstone Proposal.

Inter-Arts Minor and Honors in the Arts

If a declared Inter-Arts Minor is accepted to Honors in the Arts, they have two choices: 

A) the student may drop the minor and declare Honors in the Arts (IHN) instead, or

B) the student may pursue both the Inter-Arts Minor and Honors in the Arts, but must also complete 6 additional units of coursework, to be approved by the Faculty Director, in order to satisfy the requirements of both programs.

In senior year, any Inter-Arts Minors who have been accepted to Honors in the Arts will enroll in the Honors Capstone Workshop series (ARTSINST 201A, B, & C) for up to five units per quarter. For those students completing both the Inter-Arts Minor and Honors in the Arts, this workshop series replaces the Interdisciplinary Arts Capstone Workshop series (ARTSINST 200A, B & C).

rows.name: ASAM-BA
rows.catalogDescription: In this interdisciplinary program, you’ll have the opportunity to learn about and understand the historical and current experiences of Asian Americans, a rapidly developing, complex, and heterogeneous population for which there is neither a single identity nor community. You’ll develop skills to rigorously analyze race and ethnicity in all aspects of human life — including diversity and social justice — as you better prepare yourself to live and work in a multicultural world.

customFields.A3i6E:
The Program in Asian American Studies (AAS) was born out of the 1960s movements for third-world liberation with a mission to utilize education as a path towards a more just world. The interdisciplinary field of AAS was created in solidarity with racialized and oppressed communities, and is rooted in community-based scholarship and student activism. With a foundation of history, culture, and context, AAS students examine the diverse experiences of Asian American communities and Asian diasporas to analyze systems of power, interrogate histories of empire, war, colonialism, indigeneity, imperialism, class, sexuality, and more.

True to the liberatory tradition of ethnic studies, AAS seeks to empower students by melding scholarship, critical theory, and practice. Through classes and programming, AAS provides opportunities to engage in critical research alongside local communities, such as learning from visual artists and musicians to analyze the politics of culture, working alongside K12 students and teachers in San Jose to underscore the importance of ethnic studies in public schools, and collaborating with activist organizations in the East Bay to fight racist deportation laws. Together, our faculty and students create impactful scholarship in service to Asian American communities and beyond. 

AAS is located within the Interdepartmental Program in Comparative Studies in Race and Ethnicity (CSRE). CSRE explores how race and ethnicity shape global history, undergird our social systems, and touch every aspect of our lives. Our courses empower students with the tools to assess and build inclusivity, equity, diversity, accessibility, and justice. CCSRE programs–encompassing Asian American Studies, Chicana/o-Latina/o Studies, Comparative Studies in Race and Ethnicity, Jewish Studies, and Native American Studies–take an interdisciplinary approach to considering how gender, sexuality, ability, capital, technology, education, history, politics, and the environment structure our bodies, experiences, and communities. Students have the option to focus on particular racial and ethnic communities and on issues that move across peoples and places.

The interdisciplinary nature of the academic programs empowers students to enroll in a wide variety of courses. CCSRE listings can be found in Anthropology, Art and Art History, Education, History, Linguistics, Literature, Music, Philosophy, Political Science, Psychology, Religious Studies, Sociology, Theater and Performance Studies, and more. Majors and minors in CCSRE engage with various perspectives and methodologies and grapple with pivotal themes including decolonization, indigeneity, intersectionality, movement-building, resistance, solidarity and wellness. By analyzing interlocking structures of identity and difference, CCSRE students interrogate the role of power, reimagine the world, and reclaim the future.
customFields.WOZxr: Up to 20 units of external credit may be applied toward elective coursework in the major.
customFields.ItCSB:
The Program in Asian American Studies expects that undergraduate majors concluding their course of study will be able to:

  • Mobilize comparative frameworks for analyzing how race and ethnicity develop historically, cross-culturally, and transnationally

  • Understand, interpret, and utilize trans- and interdisciplinary theories and methods in the study of race and ethnicity

  • Critically engage with primary and secondary sources and use both types of evidence in research and argumentation

  • Effectively communicate data, research, and arguments to diverse audiences

  • Apply a core inventory of theories, methods, and concepts to local and global contexts

  • Examine the artistic, historical, humanistic, political, and social dimensions of Asian America

  • Interrogate intersections of power across multiple communities and varied identities of Asian America

rules.name: Foundations of African Studies OR Foundations of African American Studies
Community Engaged Learning
rules.description: The field of African and African American Studies has a rich history and tradition of being grounded in theory, practice, and community. The field was founded out of community demand and thus we have a social responsibility to engage in work that services Black, African, and/or African diasporic communities. The DAAAS community engaged learning requirement allows students to engage with communities to address a collective problem or societal need, critically examine public issues, and/or engage in a community-based project. This requirement allows students to either take a relevant class from one of these Community Engaged Learning course offerings via Cardinal courses (courses must have a focus on Black, African, and/or African Diasporic community/communities). Students can also choose to design their own community engaged learning experience in close collaboration with their faculty advisor and the DAAAS Director of Advanced Studies and Community Engaged Learning. This could involve an individualized and ethical strategy for engagement with an African diasporic community in the Bay Area (examples include the Congolese Community Center in Oakland; the Central African Dance Center in Richmond; the Eritrean Community Center in San Francisco, amongst many other possibilities). Students are also able to fulfill the requirement through participation in a one of Stanford’s Bing Overseas Study programs (BOSP). Either through BOSP’s Global Seminars or quarter-long Stanford-In programs, particularly the Cape Town program,  students are able to fulfill their community engaged learning requirement via participation in an overseas program that focuses on Black, African, and/or African diasporic communities. Note that a study abroad course must contain a community engaged learning component in the course to fulfill the requirement for the major.  DAAAS students must take a 2 credit “re-entry” directed readings course with their faculty advisor upon returning from an overseas study course. In connection with this community engaged requirement, students could design a public deliverable that could also become the basis for their final Capstone project or Honors thesis project.

rules.name: Capstone Experience
Honors Requirements
rules.description:
The Department of African & African American Studies honors program provides qualified DAAAS majors with the opportunity to pursue original research in their areas of interest pertaining to Black Studies or any other approach to African and African American Studies during their senior year. Students are expected to produce a paper of the highest quality reflecting three quarters of sustained effort and engagement. Over the course of their senior year, students will develop effective research skills and the ability to critically analyze data. Students will also learn how to construct persuasive arguments and to communicate their new insights with attention to both clarity and nuance, culminating in a 40-60 page honors thesis. 

To participate in the DAAAS honors program, students must average a minimum 3.5 overall GPA average. The final honors or creative honors thesis must receive a grade of an “A” in order for students to earn the honors distinction in the Department of African & African American Studies. Students must also prepare and deliver a conference-style presentation of their work during the DAAAS Senior Presentations during the Spring quarter of their senior year.  

DAAAS majors participating in the honors program must enroll in 5 units of course (the DAAAS Capstone course, which is also a WIM course) in the Autumn, 5 units of course in the Winter, and 5 units of course in the Spring. Please note that the DAAAS honors program courses (course and course) do not count toward students’ overall units required for the DAAAS major. 

The DAAAS Capstone course and two honors courses provide students with a community of peers conducting scholarly research with support from the Director of Advanced Studies and Community Engaged Learning, faculty advisors, workshop leaders, and other units on campus like the Hume Center for Writing and Speaking, as they work on their honors and creative honors theses.

rows.name: American S
rows.catalogDescription: With coursework across various topic areas — history and institutions, literature, culture and the arts, and comparative race and ethnicity — you’ll discover how different disciplines approach the study and interpretation of American life. You’ll also define and pursue your own thematic concentration in areas including feminism, gender and sexuality, anthropology, religion, sociology, education, music, film, African American, Chicana/o-Latina/o, or Native American studies.

customFields.A3i6E:
American Studies is an interdisciplinary undergraduate major that provides a rich and multifaceted understanding of American culture and society in all their complexity. Building on a foundation of core courses in history, politics, and society; literature, culture, and the arts; and race and ethnicity, students learn to analyze and interpret America’s past and present from multiple angles while also forging fresh and creative syntheses.   

Beyond the core courses, students are expected to define and pursue their interests in interpreting essential dimensions of American life. Accordingly, each student designs a unique Thematic Concentration of at least five courses drawn from fields such as history, literature, art, communication, theater, political science, African American studies, feminist studies, economics, cultural and social anthropology, Asian American studies, religious studies, Chicana/o studies, law, sociology, education, Native American studies, music, and film. Whether defined broadly or narrowly, the thematic focus or concentration should examine its subject from the vantage of multiple disciplines. Examples of thematic concentrations can be found here.

Students will conclude the major by developing a capstone project either in the Senior Colloquium or, with program approval, by pursuing an honors research project during their senior year.

Because the American Studies major cultivates an extraordinary breadth of knowledge and awareness, as well as exceptionally deft critical thinking and innovative problem-solving skills, it serves as excellent preparation for a wide range of future pursuits, including further study in graduate or professional schools and careers in journalism, government, business, law, entertainment, public service, the arts, and other fields.

Students should be aware that not all courses are offered each year; students should consult Navigate Classes for scheduling information for the current academic year.

rows.name: Anthropolo
rows.catalogDescription: Study human beings and human societies as they exist across time and space in a way distinct from other social sciences. You’ll give central attention to the entire span of human history and the full range of societies and cultures using methods especially attuned to questions of social, cultural, and biological diversity, issues of power, identity, and inequality, and the dynamic processes of social, historical, ecological, and biological change over time. Your coursework and experience deliver excellent preparation for living and working in a multicultural and globally-interconnected world.

customFields.A3i6E:
The courses offered by the Department of Anthropology are designed to:

  • provide undergraduates with instruction in anthropology;

  • provide undergraduate majors in Anthropology with a program of work leading to the bachelor’s degree; 

  • and prepare graduate candidates for advanced degrees in Anthropology.

Anthropology is devoted to the study of human beings and human societies as they exist across time and space. It is distinct from other social sciences in that it gives central attention to the entire period of human history and the full range of human societies and cultures, including those in historically marginalized parts of the world. It is, therefore, especially attuned to questions of social, cultural, and biological diversity, to issues of power, identity, and inequality, and to understanding the dynamic processes of social, historical, ecological, and biological change over time.

The Department of Anthropology offers various approaches to the topics and area studies within the field, including archaeology, ecology, environmental anthropology, evolution, linguistics, medical anthropology, political economy, science and technology studies, and sociocultural anthropology. Methodologies for studying micro- and macro-social processes are taught through qualitative and quantitative approaches. The department provides students with excellent training in theory and methods to enable them to pursue graduate study in any of the above mentioned subfields of Anthropology.

In addition to gaining an excellent foundation for graduate research and study, students majoring in Anthropology can pursue careers in government, international business, international development agencies, education, law, mass media, nonprofit organizations, and public policy.

Undergraduate training in the Department of Anthropology is only designed for students who seek a Bachelor of Arts (BA) degree. Students may declare a major in Anthropology and earn a BA degree by completing the requirements listed. The Anthropology BA degree program usually requires at least five quarters of enrollment. Eligible students may also pursue a Bachelor of Arts with Honors. 

Advising is an essential component of the Anthropology major. Students will get assigned a major advisor and are encouraged to work closely with them. Advising milestones for the major include the following:

  • In the quarter in which the major is declared, students will meet with their assigned major advisor. The Undergraduate Committee will assign a faculty appointed in the department as the student’s major advisor based on the student’s chosen emphasis. Together, the student and the major advisor will create a rigorous plan of study based on topical breadth, obtain major advisor approval of an Anthropology emphasis as part of the plan of study, and obtain the major advisor’s signature on the Major Form.

  • Undergraduate Anthropology majors should plan to meet with their major advisor at least once each quarter before the final study list deadline. The faculty advisor must approve any revisions to the initial checklist.

  • Undergraduate Anthropology majors must submit an updated and approved Major Form to the undergraduate student services officer in the quarter before graduating.

Please note your major advisor does not necessarily have to be your honors thesis advisor. It is encouraged that you connect and cultivate a relationship with a faculty advisor who could serve and oversee your research. If you have any questions, please contact the Undergraduate SSO.

rules.name: Honors Program
rules.description:
The Honors Program in Anthropology provides eligible Anthropology majors with an opportunity to conduct original ethnographic, field, laboratory, or library-based research under the guidance of an Anthropology faculty member. As an honor’s candidate, you will have the opportunity to conduct real research and experience what it is like to write anthropological pieces. It will also help you develop and enhance your analytical and writing skills. 

QUALIFICATIONS

  • Declared Anthropology Major 

  • 3.4 GPA in the Major and a 3.0 GPA in overall coursework. 

  • No more than one “Incomplete” may be listed on the transcript.

HOW TO APPLY

  • Deadline to apply via the form on the department website is typically the Friday of Week 1 of Spring quarter during Junior Year. If accepted to the Honors Program by the Undergraduate Committee in Junior Year, apply for Honors on Axess beginning of Winter Quarter of Senior Year.

  • Please note your major advisor does not necessarily have to be your honors thesis advisor. It is encouraged to connect with a faculty member who could serve as your honors thesis advisor and oversee your research. If you have any questions, please contact the Undergraduate SSO if you have questions.

REQUIREMENTS

  • Students interested in the Honors Program must consult the department website for timeline, course requirements, and paper guidelines including funding opportunities available for summer quarter research. In most cases, honors students apply for funding early in their junior year.

  • Students must also enroll in ANTHRO95B (Independent Study for Honors or Senior Paper Writing) in the final quarter of the undergraduate degree program and earn a grade of A- or better to graduate with honors.

rows.catalogDescription: Complement your PhD studies in a related field with graduate coursework in Anthropology to earn a PhD minor in this field of study.

customFields.A3i6E:
Anthropology is devoted to the study of human beings and human societies as they exist across time and space. It is distinct from other social sciences in that it gives central attention to the full time span of human history, and to the full range of human societies and cultures, including those located in historically marginalized parts of the world. It is therefore especially attuned to questions of social, cultural, and biological diversity, to issues of power, identity, and inequality, and to the understanding of dynamic processes of social, historical, ecological, and biological change over time. Education in anthropology provides excellent preparation for living in a multicultural and globally-interconnected world, and helps to equip students for careers in fields including law, medicine, business, public service, research, and ecological sustainability and resource management.

The Department of Anthropology offers a wide range of approaches to the various topics and area studies within anthropology including: archaeology, ecology, environmental anthropology, evolution, linguistics, medical anthropology, political economy, science and technology studies, and sociocultural anthropology. Methodologies for the study of micro- and macro-social processes are taught through the use of qualitative and quantitative approaches. The department provides students with excellent training in theory and methods to enable them to pursue graduate study in any of the above mentioned subfields of anthropology.

To request the PhD minor in Anthropology:

  1. Identify a PhD minor advisor from the Department of Anthropology tenure-line faculty. 

    • The Department of Anthropology requires the PhD minor advisor to serve as a member on the student's dissertation reading committee and university oral examination committee.

  2. Submit the following forms and paperwork to the department Student Services Manager for review by the Department of Anthropology Director of Graduate Studies (DGS)

    • Signed Anthropology, PhD Minor Plan of Study Form 

    • Approved pre-dissertation or dissertation proposal

  3. Submit a university application for PhD minor, outlining a program of study approved by the major and minor departments, via Axess eForms (at the time of admission to candidacy) once the PhD minor is approved by the Anthropology DGS.

rows.name: Archaeolog
rows.catalogDescription: Learn to analyze human heritage and bridge former and present societies by examining the past through its material remains. You’ll get direct access to the experiences of a wide range of people in numerous cultures across the globe through an interdisciplinary approach that draws in equal parts on the humanities, social sciences, and natural sciences.

customFields.A3i6E:
Archaeology is the study of human societies through their material remains, offering direct access to the experiences of a wide range of people in numerous cultures across the globe. Increasingly, archaeology bridges past and present societies through the study of the human heritage and its role in contemporary societies. 

The mission of Stanford’s undergraduate program in Archaeology is to provide students with a broad and rigorous interdisciplinary approach to the analysis of the material culture of past societies, drawing on the questions and methods of the humanities, social sciences, and natural sciences, and including the faculty and courses from a wide range of University departments and programs. Students in the major learn to relate these analyses to the practice of archaeology in the contemporary world. The program seeks to help each student achieve a high level of understanding through concentrated study of a particular research area. Archaeology students are well prepared for advanced training in professional and graduate schools.
customFields.WOZxr: If you would like to submit a course petition request for courses outside of Stanford, contact the Archaeology student services officer.
customFields.ItCSB:
Learning outcomes are used in evaluating students and the department’s undergraduate program. The department expects undergraduate students in the program to be able to demonstrate the following learning outcomes:

  1. Develop critical thinking skills in relation to diverse human societies and histories.

  2. Form an understanding of the history of thought and theoretical foundations of archaeology.

  3. Develop a familiarity with the different kinds of methods and evidence that archaeologists use to make arguments about the past.  

  4. Investigate specialized knowledge of the archaeology of a particular topic or region.

  5. Develop the ability to clearly and persuasively communicate ideas about archaeology to multiple audiences and communities.

  6. Develop an appreciation of the ways in which archaeological practice, methods, and knowledge can contribute to addressing contemporary social issues and problems.

requisitesSimple.name: Narrative Text
requisitesSimple.notes:
Degree Requirements Overview:

Coursework must form a coherent program of study, and be approved by the student services officer and the program faculty director. The degree requirements are divided into six components. A course may only be used once to fulfill a degree component and may only be used to satisfy requirements for one major.

Students must meet the minimum unit count totaling 65 units:

  • Core | 15 Units

  • Methods & Skills: Statistics | 5 Units

  • Methods & Skills | 10 Units

  • Theory | 10 Units

  • Electives | 20 Units

  • Capstone | 5 Units

Undergraduates may fulfill course requirements in Methods & Skills, Theory, and Electives from graduate-level courses with the approval of the instructor and Archaeology Center director.

requisitesSimple.name: Core Program Requirements

rules.name: Core
rules.description:
All three courses must be taken for a letter grade and have a minimum passing grade of B. Completing these three courses should amount to 15 units.

course (Introduction to Archaeology) is recommended as a first course. Many upper-level courses in Archaeology require this course as a prerequisite.

rules.name: Methods & Skills: Statistics
rules.description:
Quantitative skills and computing ability are indispensable to archaeologists. Students must take one statistics course for five units to fulfill the statistics requirement.

Courses taken to fulfill the statistics component cannot be used to satisfy any other degree requirement. A course can only be applied to one degree component.

rules.name: Methods & Skills
rules.description:
To fulfill the Methods & Skills component, students must take courses on archaeological Methods & Skills, ten units.

Methods & Skills courses may include archaeological formation processes, botanical analysis, cartography, ceramic analysis, dating methods, faunal analysis, geographic information systems, geology, geophysics, genetics, osteology, remote sensing, soil chemistry, and statistics, among other topics. 

Courses taken to fulfill the Methods & Skills component cannot be used to satisfy any other degree requirement. A course can only be applied to one degree component.

rules.name: Theory
rules.description:
Students must take ten units from any course designated explicitly as Theory. Courses in this area may include archaeological, art-historical, sociocultural, historical, and material culture theory. 

Courses taken to fulfill the Theory component cannot be used to satisfy any other degree requirement. A course can only be applied to one degree component.

rules.name: Required Milestone: Archaeological Field Experiences
rules.description: Students must take part in a field experience approved by the Stanford Archaeology Center, and enroll in any coursework that is required for participation in the field experience. Experiences are typically offered during summer months and funding may be provided. Other opportunities to fulfill the field experience requirement may include on campus field schools provided by the Center. Students may also petition for exemption to this requirement, but the exemption will normally be granted only in exceptional circumstances. Read more about Field Experiences here.

rules.name: Required Milestone: Senior Capstone
rules.description: Students must complete a Senior Capstone and have three options for doing so: an Honors Thesis, a SUAC project, or a Senior Project. Students typically complete the capstone requirement their senior year while enrolled in the required course ARCHLGY 130: Senior Capstone. ARCHLGY 130 can be taken for variable units across multiple quarters, but students must earn at least 5 units total.

requisitesSimple.notes:
Related Courses

Archaeology is an interdisciplinary program. Students should meet with their advisor about degree requirements and the applicability of courses from other university departments to the Archaeology major or minor. Applicable courses are commonly found in History (HISTORY), Anthropology (ANTHRO), Classics (CLASSICS), and East Asian Languages and Cultures (EALC) but are not limited to these departments. Students should consult their advisor and the program director for course approvals. 

Overseas Studies Courses in Archaeology

For course descriptions and additional offerings, see the Bing Overseas Studies website listings. Students should consult their department or program’s student services office for the applicability of Overseas Studies courses to a major or minor program.

rules.description:
Students must complete 20 units of Electives on regions, themes, or other areas of interest. They are encouraged to do so by consulting with their faculty advisor and the Archaeology SSO to design a course plan.

The electives are broken down into emphasis categories below allowing students to identify courses based on their varied interests in archaeology, and students may choose courses from multiple emphasis categories. 

  • Heritage: Courses for students interested in understanding the roles and reception of past material culture in present-day societies and cultures, navigating tensions that emerge within local, national, and international governments/communities and exploring how heritage work can contribute to healing and reconciliation.

  • Biological & Environmental Archaeology: Courses for students interested in understanding how humans lived and interacted with their surroundings and the environment.

  • Archaeological Science & Technology: Courses for students interested in how the sciences and technologies applied to material culture help us understand past societies.

  • Materiality & Society: Courses for students interested in the relationship and interaction between humans, their objects, and the societies they built together. 

  • Regional: Courses for students interested in a particular region of the world such as the Americas, Mediterranean, Asia/East Asia, and Africa.

Non-ARCHLGY courses can be used to fulfill this requirement with the prior approval of the Archaeology curriculum committee and Archaeology Center director. Please contact the Archaeology student services officer for more information on this petition process.

Courses taken to fulfill the elective component cannot be used to satisfy any other degree requirement. A course can only be applied to one degree component.

subRules.name: Senior Capstone Seminar for Archaeology Majors
subRules.description:
ARCHLGY 130 is a variable unit course (1-5 units). Students can take the course in multiple quarters during their senior year adding up to the required 5 units.

It must be taken as part of any of the three Capstone options below.

subRules.name: Option 1: Honors Thesis
subRules.description: 1. The honors program in Archaeology gives qualified majors a chance to work closely with faculty on an individual research project culminating in an honors thesis. Students may begin honors research from several starting points, including topics introduced in the core or upper-division courses, independent interests, research on artifacts in Stanford’s collections, or fieldwork experiences. Interested Archaeology majors of junior standing may apply for admission by submitting an honors application form, including a four to five-page statement of the project, a transcript, and a letter of recommendation from the faculty member supervising the honors thesis. Applications are due by May 1st of their junior year. Archaeology majors are eligible to apply for honors candidacy. The thesis is due in early May of their senior year. It is read by the candidate’s advisor and a second reader. Students will be invited to present at the SAC Spring Symposium in May or may arrange to present their research results in another public forum.

subRules.name: Option 2: SUAC Project
subRules.description: Students interested in working on a SUAC Capstone Project with the Stanford University Archaeology Collections (SUAC) can do so individually or as a team. Projects are tailored to the student’s interest within the scope of current initiatives underway at SUAC. Students will work with staff at SUAC and their faculty mentor at SAC. Projects may take various creative forms, such as deep research or materials analysis of a particular artifact, research reports on sites or collections, or the development of a virtual or physical exhibit. Students will be invited to present at the SAC Spring Symposium in May or may arrange to present their research results in another public forum.

subRules.name: Option 3: Senior Project
subRules.description: The Senior Project is for students who want to design their capstone individually or as part of a team. Students will participate in ARCHLGY 130, Senior Capstone Seminar for Archaeology Majors to explore their ideas and begin developing a project proposal. During the winter quarter, students will start and/or continue the research and development of the project. Students will be invited to present at the SAC Spring Symposium in May or may arrange to present their research results in another public forum.

rules.name: Capstone Requirement
rules.description:
Students will have three options for their capstone requirement, and all will have to enroll in a Senior Capstone Seminar (ARCHLGY 130) course for 5 units.

ARCHLGY 130: Senior Capstone Seminar for Archaeology Majors is offered to students in their final year of study as either a stand-alone course on designing research projects and writing or as a touchpoint for students who are launching the writing phase of their senior projects or honors thesis.

The honors program in Archaeology gives qualified majors a chance to work closely with faculty on an individual research project culminating in an honors thesis. Students may begin honors research from several starting points, including topics introduced in the core or upper-division courses, independent interests, research on artifacts in Stanford’s collections, or fieldwork experiences.

Interested Archaeology majors of junior standing may apply for admission by submitting an honors application form, including a 4-5 page statement of the project, a transcript, and a letter of recommendation from the faculty member supervising the honors thesis. Archaeology majors are eligible to apply for honors candidacy. The thesis is due in early May of the senior year and is read by the candidate’s advisor and a second reader.

Applications are due in mid-May of your junior year. Contact the Student Services Officer for more information.

rows.catalogDescription: This relatively small doctoral program affords you the opportunity to work intensively with faculty in a specialized area you choose as you pursue an advanced degree. Your coursework further enhances your existing background and experience in the general history of art.

customFields.A3i6E:
Doctor of Philosophy in Art History

The doctoral program in Art & Art History provides students with rigorous training in researching and analyzing visual and material cultures, including Film and Media Studies. The program prepares students to produce original scholarship and to teach art history at advanced academic levels.

This program is full-time. Doctoral students in the Art History PhD program are expected to maintain a significant physical presence on campus throughout their graduate studies. This ensures that students have access to advisors and mentors, libraries, and other resources that support timely progress towards completion of degree requirements. Additionally, being on campus ensures that students are part of the academic and campus community, which supports continued professional development
customFields.WOZxr: Students who completed graduate coursework at another institution may transfer course units (up to 45) in the winter quarter of their first year of doctoral study. Graduate work accepted for transfer of credit does not automatically exempt a student from having to complete a course requirement for the degree.
customFields.ItCSB: The PhD is conferred upon candidates in Art History, including Film and Media Studies, who have demonstrated substantial scholarship and the ability to conduct independent research and analysis in their respective disciplines. By completing advanced coursework and skills training, the doctoral program prepares students to make original contributions to knowledge in their fields and interpret and present their research results.
customFields.advisingExpectations:
The Department of Art and Art History is committed to providing academic advising in support of graduate students' scholarly and professional development. When most effective, this advising relationship entails collaborative and sustained engagement by the advisor and the advisee.  Students are encouraged to communicate clearly and frequently with their advisors, meeting with their assigned advisor at least once a quarter.

Both the advisor and the advisee are expected to maintain professionalism and integrity. Should serious challenges arise in the advising relationship, the advisee and advisor (together or individually) should confer with the Director of Graduate Studies (DGS) and/or Department Chair.

Faculty advisors guide students in critical areas such as selecting courses, designing and conducting research, developing teaching pedagogy, navigating policies and degree requirements, and exploring academic opportunities and professional pathways.

Graduate students are active contributors to the advising relationship, proactively seeking academic and professional guidance and taking responsibility for informing themselves of policies and degree requirements for their graduate program.

customFields.programGradingPolicies:
Graduate students in the department must take required courses for letter grades if this option is available, and are expected to earn a grade of 'B+' or above in each course. Any grade of 'B' or below is considered to be less than satisfactory.

Students are responsible for making sure grades are reported. If asterisks (*), incomplete grades (I), GNR, or No Credits (NC) appear on the end-of-quarter grade report, students should check with their instructor immediately.
customFields.programGPARequirement: Graduate students in the department are required to maintain a GPA of 3.0 in all courses required for the degree. Students with a GPA of less than 3.0 are not making satisfactory progress and may be at risk for dismissal from the program.

rules.name: Collateral Studies
rules.notes:
Collaterals are courses offered outside the Art & Art History Department that complement a student’s area of concentration. These courses strengthen the student’s interdisciplinary study of art history. 

Students entering with a B.A. must take a minimum of three collateral courses. Those entering with an M.A. must take a minimum of two collateral courses. If appropriate, one collateral may be a course in studio art. 

Students must consult with their primary advisor about their choice of collateral courses prior to their enrollment. Students must complete their collaterals by the end of the spring quarter of the third year.

NOTE: Courses cross-listed with ARTHIST or FILMEDIA do not fulfill this requirement.

rules.name: Distribution Requirements
rules.description:
The department offers two distribution requirement tracks: Art History and Film & Media Studies.

The Art History track has five areas of distribution:

  • 1000 BCE-13th Century

  • 14th Century-17th Century

  • 18th Century - Present

  • Film & Media Studies

  • Asian/African/Islamic/Indigenous

Students must take at least one course in each of the five distribution areas.

The Film & Media Studies track has five areas of distribution:

  • Theories of Cinema

  • Media Studies

  • Art History

  • National Cinemas (includes international)

  • Form, Function, and Aesthetics

Students must take at least one course in each of the five distribution areas.

Fulfilling the distribution requirement with graduate seminars is strongly encouraged. If students have entered the Stanford program with an MA, they may transfer courses taken at the graduate level to fulfill up to two areas of the distribution requirement.

All courses must be taught by different faculty members. Students are strongly encouraged to fulfill the distribution requirement with graduate seminars taken for 5 units.

The qualifying exam should ideally be taken by the end of winter quarter in the student’s third year of PhD study.  (Students entering the program with an MA should aim to take it in the fall quarter of the third year.) The exam consists of a written and an oral component. Each portion of the exam is administered on separate days during the same week, with the written portion taking place first. Both parts of the exam are graded on a High Pass/Pass/Fail system. 

To prepare for the exam, students may enroll in up to two 5-8 unit exam preparation courses (ARTHIST620), one per quarter.

If a student fails one or both parts of the exam, they are allowed to retake that portion or portions of the exam they have failed. For a detailed account of the written and oral exam format, see the Graduate Student Handbook for the Department of Art and Art History.
rules.name: Qualifying Exam
Graduate Pedagogy
rules.description: Students are required to take ARTHIST405A Graduate Pedagogy. This course is offered every other academic year,ideally taken either before or during a student’s first teaching assistantship.

Students are required to complete three quarters of teaching experiences. Students can complete more than the required number of teaching quarters, given availability.

At least one teaching experience  must be in a course from the following list:

  • ARTHIST 1A

  • ARTHIST 1B

  • ARTHIST 2

  • ARTHIST 3

  • ARTHIST 5

  • FILMEDIA 4
rules.name: Graduate Student Teaching

rules.description: Teaching is core to the academic and professional training of doctoral students in our program. All students are required to complete 3 quarters of teaching experience by the end of their third year in the program regardless of their financial support. Students may teach additional quarters beyond the degree requirement as part of their professional training and financial support.
rules.name: Teaching Requirement
Advancement to Candidacy
rules.description:
At the end of the spring quarter of the second year, faculty formally review graduate students’ progress to determine whether they meet the requirements for candidacy. 

To apply for candidacy, students must submit a file at the beginning of the spring quarter of their second year demonstrating that they have completed all candidacy requirements. Students entering the program with an MA are encouraged to apply earlier during the autumn quarter of their second year. All students must advance to candidacy by the spring quarter of the second year.

Candidacy requirements (as further detailed in the department’s Graduate Handbook) include:

  • Completion of all language requirements

  • Completion of all distribution requirements

  • Completion of all collateral requirements

  • Completion of 45 units of coursework

The graduate student does not become a formal candidate for the PhD degree until they have satisfied these requirements and the faculty has voted to confer candidacy. Failure to advance to candidacy may result in the student’s dismissal from the program.

Additional details on qualifying procedures can be found in the Graduate Handbook <https://artgradguide.stanford.edu/phd-programs/candidacy-phd-degree>.

rules.value:
In the Department of Art & Art History, the oral exam is a defense of the dissertation presented upon the completion of a substantial portion of the dissertation or upon completion of a pre-final draft. Students consult with their dissertation advisor and reading committee members on the timing of the defense. The department generally expects this milestone to be completed within five years of the student's admission to PhD candidacy.

The oral defense consists primarily of a presentation and critical dissertation discussion but may range, at the committee’s discretion, over a wider field. The student is expected to describe dissertation research methods and findings at some length and to answer all questions and criticisms put by members of the examining committee. At the end of the defense, the committee votes to pass or fail the student on the defense. 

In the case of failure on the defense, the examiners may establish criteria for reconsidering a resubmitted dissertation. If the defense is passed, the committee may recommend changes in the dissertation manuscript before submitting it to the university as the final requirement for granting the PhD. After incorporating these changes, the student's principal advisor gives the manuscript a last review and approval.
rules.name: Oral Defense of the Dissertation
Dissertation Colloquium
rules.description:
The department requires a total of three colloquia to be facilitated between the graduate student and their reading committee. 

The proposal colloquium is held after the dissertation proposal is fully drafted. At this stage, the advisor and dissertation committee meet with the student to discuss and provide feedback on the proposal prior to its final approval and signing. 

The first chapter colloquium is a required review of the first completed dissertation chapter. The dissertation colloquium is held on the completed or near-completed dissertation prior to submission and defense.

rules.name: Dissertation Proposal
rules.description:
By the beginning of the autumn quarter in the fourth year, students should have identified a dissertation topic and prepared a proposal in consultation with their principal faculty advisor.

The proposal must be 12–15 pages in length, excluding the bibliography and appendix of images. Students may enroll in ARTHIST 640 (5 units) to prepare the proposal.

The student must submit the dissertation proposal directly to their dissertation reading committee for review and approval. This should happen no later than early November of the autumn quarter in the student's fourth year of study.

If the proposal is not approved, the Faculty Committee will specify the conditions for its revision, resubmission, and reconsideration.

rules.name: Dissertation
rules.description: Students are required to submit an approved dissertation that makes an original contribution to the field of Art History. Students are expected to submit their final dissertation in the same quarter as the oral defense. The department generally expects the dissertation to be completed within five years of the student's admission to PhD candidacy. The final draft of the dissertation must be submitted to the dissertation reading committee at least four weeks before the oral defense.

Graduate students must demonstrate proficiency in one language relevant to their field of study. Students focusing on Western Art typically satisfy this requirement by demonstrating reading proficiency in a European language. Students focusing on Asian Art typically satisfy this requirement by demonstrating proficiency in an Asian language.

The language requirement should be satisfied by the end of the second year of study. Students entering the PhD program with an M.A. are expected to have satisfied the language requirement before admission.

The language requirement may be fulfilled by passing a reading examination administered through the Stanford Language Center or by demonstrating equivalent proficiency through Stanford language coursework, as determined by the faculty. Students who satisfy the requirement through coursework must complete the course for a letter grade (when that option is available) and submit a letter from the instructor confirming reading proficiency.

rows.catalogDescription: Your undergraduate degree coursework in Art History prepares you to understand works of art, architecture, and design from various perspectives, including the original context of their making and reception and their subsequent circulation, collection, conservation, and display.

customFields.A3i6E: The undergraduate program is designed to help students think critically about the visual arts and visual culture. Courses focus on the meaning of images and media and their historical development, societal roles, and relationships to disciplines such as literature, music, political science, religion, and philosophy. Work performed in the classroom, studio, and screening room is designed to develop a student’s powers of perception, capacity for visual analysis, and knowledge of technical processes.
customFields.WOZxr: Students can take a maximum of two courses (10 units) away from Stanford; this includes transfer courses from other universities and Stanford Bing Overseas Studies Program. Students must meet with their faculty advisor and the Student Services Specialist before planning an overseas campus program.
customFields.ItCSB:
The department expects undergraduate majors in the program to be able to demonstrate the following learning outcomes. These learning outcomes are used in evaluating students and the department’s undergraduate program.

Students are expected to demonstrate:

  • Knowledge of artistic and architectural movements and related sociohistorical events.

  • Ability to develop compelling and nuanced lines of interpretation about artworks, buildings, and material cultures.

  • Improvement in critical thinking skills using primary and secondary sources.

  • Improvement in writing and close reading skills.

  • Ability to evaluate artworks, buildings, and sites through knowledge of specialized language and concepts.

rules.name: Overview and Course
rules.description:
The purpose of the honors program is to extend and deepen work done in Art History classes. The honors thesis topic typically emerges from prior coursework; it should be focused and have clear parameters. Ordinarily, an honors thesis is an exploration of an area the student has already studied.

Admission to the Honor Program

The minimum requirement for admission to the honors program is an overall GPA of 3.5 and at least 3.5 in Art History courses. Students must complete at least five Art History courses at Stanford by the end of their junior year, and four must be completed by the end of Winter Quarter.

Submission of the Thesis Proposal

Candidates for the honors program must submit a five-page (double-spaced) thesis proposal, including bibliography and illustrations, and one completed paper that demonstrates the student’s ability to conceptualize and write cogently about art historical issues. A complete application is due to the proposed thesis advisor on March 31.

Submission and Approval of the Honors Thesis

Students must submit the final draft of their honors thesis to their faculty advisor, the second faculty reader, the Student Services Specialist, and the Honors Director by the thesis deadline. 

More Information

For more information about the Art History and Film & Media Studies Honors Program, students can visit the department website.

rows.catalogDescription: Prepare for a career in the visual arts and hone your creative capabilities. This flexible program delivers diverse courses, a production-based curriculum, and cross-disciplinary interaction with faculty and fellow students that exposes you to a broad range of art forms, their cultural and historical uses, impact, production, and circulation. You’ll also become familiar with various studio facilities and gain experience with group critiques and exhibition practices.

customFields.A3i6E: The undergraduate program in Art Practice is designed to help students develop contemporary art practice making skills and think critically about the visual arts and visual culture. Courses focus on the meaning of images and media and their historical development, societal roles, and relationships to disciplines such as literature, music, and philosophy. Work performed in the classroom, studio, and screening room is designed to develop a student’s powers of perception, capacity for visual analysis, and knowledge of technical processes.

customFields.ItCSB:
The department expects undergraduate majors in the program to be able to demonstrate the following learning outcomes. These learning outcomes are used in evaluating students and the department’s undergraduate program.

Students in the Art Practice major are expected to demonstrate:

  • Enhanced awareness of the role of art in intellectual and cultural life

  • Problem-solving skills to organize, analyze, and interpret visual information

  • Mastery of techniques and materials of a discipline with awareness of historical and current practices

  • Selection of materials, processes, form, and content to achieve poetic and expressive relationships to artistic media

  • Ability to apply critical analysis to the student’s own work and the work of others

  • Effective techniques for preparing and presenting work consistent with professional practices in the field

customFields.z8ch4: Students considering an Art Practice major are encouraged to take the following three introductory courses, which also fulfill major requirements, during their frosh or sophomore years. The core studio series  course - Foundations 2D and course - Foundations 3D/4D expose students to a broad range of contemporary artists and hands-on art-making techniques, familiarize students with the various studio facilities in the Department of Art & Art History, introduce key theoretical concepts in contemporary practice, and provide experience with group critiques and exhibition practices which are critical components of the art practice field and major. ARTHIST5 - Art and Power familiarizes students with contemporary thinking regarding the power dynamics in the production and circulation of art, along with its cultural and historical uses and impacts. rules.description:
The Department of Art & Art History’s year-long Honors Program allows selected Art Practice majors to develop a self-initiated body of thesis artwork throughout their senior year in parallel with their regular work for the Art Practice major.  The body of thesis artwork students propose and develop is expected to deepen and elaborate on work and themes they have begun to explore in previous courses or independent work. This thesis artwork is exhibited in an honors exhibition in the early Spring of the senior year. Students also produce a written thesis paper contextualizing and documenting this work. 

The Honors Program is open to Art Practice majors in their senior year who are studying on campus for the entire year. Admission to the Honors Program is decided by the Art Practice faculty via a competitive application process in Spring of the junior year. Completion of the Honors Program is noted on the student’s diploma and transcript.

Participation in the Honors Program requires 10 units of honors-specific coursework dedicated to producing the thesis artwork, exhibition, and written thesis. Up to 4 units of this honors coursework may count towards one of the four upper-level elective courses required for the major. The Honors Program requires a minimum of 71 total credits, an additional 6 units beyond the 65-unit requirement for the Art Practice major.

While Art Practice honors students are expected to work independently to develop artwork for the thesis exhibition, they are supported via ongoing one-on-one tutorials with a faculty thesis mentor (which comprise 3 of the required 10 honors units) and via a year-long honors seminar with other honors students and the Director of the Honors Program (which comprise the remaining 7 required units). In the seminar, students engage with their honors cohort through critiques, visiting artists meetings, and other activities determined by the Honors Director. 

During the Honors Program, to support honors students in producing their thesis work, students are typically given access to studio space in a shared honors studio, a materials stipend, and ongoing access to McMurtry Building area-specific studios (photography, sculpture, digital media, printmaking, painting) for which they have received training.

Admission to the Honors Program

To be eligible to apply for honors:

  • Students must be in residence on campus all of their senior year. 

  • Students must have completed course - Foundations I, course - Foundations II, course - Art & Power, and at least five Art Practice classes by the end of junior year. 

    • Four must be completed by the end of Winter Quarter junior year when the honors application is submitted. 

Detailed instructions for applying to the Honors Program during the Spring Quarter of junior year are listed on the Department of Art & Art History’s website. 

Early in their junior year, students considering honors should contact Student Services to review the requirements and express interest in the program so that they will be notified of that year’s specific application deadlines and submission process.

The application includes a portfolio, project proposal, study plan, unofficial transcript, and signature of a full-time art practice faculty member who has advised the student on their honors application project proposal. 

Students are selected for the Honors Program based on the strength of their application portfolio and project proposal. Students accepted into the Honors Program have illustrated their ability to work independently and rigorously on their artwork, participate productively in group critiques, and work respectfully in a shared studio space. The body of work students propose and develop for an honors exhibition is expected to deepen and elaborate on work and themes they have begun to explore in previous courses or independent work. 

Honors Program Requirements

The Art Practice program requires students to develop a sustained studio practice across Fall and Winter Quarters in order to generate a body of thesis artwork approved by their Honors Faculty Mentor and the Honors Director. In the Spring Quarter, this body of thesis work must be successfully installed and exhibited in the thesis exhibition and documented and analyzed through the student’s written thesis document. Students must maintain an A- in all honors course components every quarter to achieve honors on the student’s transcript.

A minimum A- grade in both honors course components (ARTSTUDI 297, 297S) must be achieved each quarter to continue in honors each quarter.

Students must also pass a faculty review at the end of Fall Quarter with the Honors Director and their Faculty Mentor to continue in the Honors Program through Winter and Spring Quarters

  • Artwork presented at the review must represent significant progress towards the student’s proposed thesis artwork.

  • Students who do not pass this review will continue as regular Art Practice majors, but not as part of the Honors Program. In this case, credits obtained for the fall Honors Faculty Tutorial and Honors Seminar will count as regular elective credits towards the Art Practice major.

Continuing in honors past Winter Quarter is conditional upon the student’s body of thesis work being ready for the honors exhibition, as evaluated by the Honors Director, the student’s Faculty Mentor, and the Gallery Director.

During the Spring Quarter, students must successfully participate in the honors exhibition, with work approved by the Honors Director and their Faculty Mentor, and delivered and installed in a professional manner with the direction of the Gallery Director.

The written thesis, including multiple iterative drafts, must be successfully completed and submitted by the deadline set by the Honors Director in the Spring Quarter.

rules.description:
The Biology minor requires a minimum of six courses meeting the following criteria:

  • All courses must be taken for a letter grade (no other grading basis is allowed).

    • A minimum total GPA of 2.0 is required in courses taken for the minor.

  • All courses must be worth or approved for three or more units.

  • At least three courses must be taken at the 100-level or higher. The only courses below 100 that are allowable are one additional BIO 80- level course and OSPAUSTL 10, 28, or 32; note that OSPAUSTL 10, 28, and 32 together count as three courses toward the minor

  • The two required 80-series courses for the minor cannot be substituted through transfer credit or any other course (BIO 100-level or higher, approved out-of-department course, or through a submitted General Petition)

  • Courses used to fulfill the minor may not be used to satisfy any other department degree requirements (minor or major).

  • Stanford Introductory Seminars (IntroSems or Sophomore Seminars) may not be used to fulfill the minor requirements.

Courses that do NOT count toward the minor:

  • Foundational lab courses (BIO 43, BIO 44, BIO 45, BIO 46, BIO 47)

  • Capstone courses: BIO 196A, 196B, 196C; BIO 199A, 199B, 199C; BIO 199W

  • Out-of-department research (BIO 199X)

  • Directed reading (BIO 198, 198X)

  • No transfer courses can count toward the BIO 80-series

customFields.advisingExpectations:
The Department of Biology is committed to providing academic advising that supports graduate students’ scholarly and professional development. When most effective, this advising relationship entails collaborative and sustained engagement by both the advisor and the advisee.

Advising is available for all MS students. There are two departmental sources for advising:

1. Faculty Advising – faculty advisors assist students in planning a coherent program of study and must sign off on the required Program Proposal. The student is responsible for finding an advisor from the Department of Biology. Signed program proposals must be submitted by all MS students.

2. Staff Advising – The graduate student services manager in the Student Services Office (Gilbert 118) is available to help students with administrative matters including, but not limited to, petitioning requirements, reviewing course schedules, and advising about the general requirements for the MS degree.

Resources for finding a faculty advisor are available online at https://biology.stanford.edu/people/faculty

Graduate students are active contributors to the advising relationship.

As a best practice, advising expectations should be periodically discussed and reviewed to ensure mutual understanding. Both the advisor and the advisee are expected to maintain professionalism and integrity.

The program director and staff monitor academic progress and student completion of program requirements and milestones.

Additionally, the program adheres to the advising guidelines and responsibilities listed by the Office of the Vice Provost for Graduate Education (VPGE), in the Graduate Academic Policies (GAP), and in Graduate Advising.

rules.name: Requirements Overview
rules.notes:
The MS program consists of Department of Biology and/or Hopkins Marine Station course work, approved out-of-department electives, and foundational breadth courses totaling at least 45 units at or above the 100-level distributed as follows:

  • At least 23 of the 45 units must be courses designated primarily for graduate students.

  • These 45 units can be chosen among offerings in the Department of Biology (BIO), the list of approved out-of-department electives (outlined below), research, teaching, and/or foundational breadth courses.

    • A maximum of 18 units may be a combination of Biology research, directed reading, and/or teaching

  • Other Stanford coursework relevant to a student’s professional development may be no more than nine units. Using the General Petition form, students must petition for courses that fall into this category.

Each candidate designs a coherent program of study in consultation with their department advisor. Although no specific courses are required, program proposals must adhere to department parameters.

In addition to the unit requirements outlined above, students must adhere to the following:

  • A program proposal, signed by the student’s advisor.

  • Students may take only six units CR/NC. (This is separate from Satisfactory/No Credit. There is no limit to Satisfactory/No Credit)

  • Students must maintain a GPA of 3.0 or higher.

  • Students must receive a B- or better grade in all courses taken for the degree.

Students not meeting these minimum requirements are subject to departmental academic review and/or dismissal.

rows.name: BIOC-MS
rows.catalogDescription: Prepare for your exciting career in biochemistry through advanced coursework and foundational discovery. You’ll learn how to pursue transformative advances in biology that uncover new principles and impact disease through research that ranges from molecular structure to organismal biology while becoming a scientist and scientific leader, as well as a member of a robust scientific community.

customFields.A3i6E:
Biochemistry is a department within the School of Medicine, with offices and labs in the Beckman Center for Molecular and Genetic Medicine at the Stanford Medical Center, the Shriram Center for Bioengineering and Chemical Engineering, and the Stanford Genome Technology Center.

The Department of Biochemistry focuses on the molecular basis of life by studying the structures and functions of proteins and nucleic acids, the control of development, molecular motors and the cytoskeleton, trafficking of proteins between organelles, regulation of gene expression, protein homeostasis, structure and design, genetic and epigenetic control of chromosome function, and the application of genomics, all toward the understanding of health and disease.

rows.name: BIOC-PHD
rows.catalogDescription: This advanced degree program opens the door to working with world-renowned faculty in advanced research facilities. With an emphasis on training in research, the program prepares you as both a scientist and a scientific leader. You’ll pursue transformative advances that uncover new principles and impact diseases.

customFields.A3i6E:
Biochemistry is a department within the School of Medicine, with offices and labs in the Beckman Center for Molecular and Genetic Medicine at the Stanford Medical Center, the Shriram Center for Bioengineering and Chemical Engineering, and the Stanford Genome Technology Center. Undergraduates and graduate and medical school students may take courses the department offers.

The Department of Biochemistry focuses on the molecular basis of life by studying the structures and functions of proteins and nucleic acids, the control of development, molecular motors and the cytoskeleton, trafficking of proteins between organelles, regulation of gene expression, protein homeostasis, structure and design, genetic and epigenetic control of chromosome function, and the application of genomics, all toward the understanding of health and disease. Advanced courses in more specialized areas emphasize the most recent developments in biochemistry, biophysics, cell biology, and molecular biology. These courses include the physical chemistry of proteins and nucleic acids, membrane biology and biochemistry, the cytoskeleton, mechanisms and regulation of nucleic acid replication and recombination, the biochemistry of bacterial and animal viruses, the molecular basis of morphogenesis, and the structure and function of both eukaryotic and prokaryotic chromosomes.

The Department of Biochemistry offers a PhD program that begins in Autumn quarter of each year. The program of study is designed to prepare students for productive careers in biochemistry; its emphasis is training in research, and each student works closely with faculty members. Opportunities exist for directed reading and research in biochemistry and molecular biology using the most advanced research facilities, including those for light and electron microscopy, chromatography and electrophoresis, protein and nucleic acid purification, rapid kinetic analysis, synthesis and analysis, single-molecule analyses using laser light traps, microarray generation and analysis, and computer graphic workstation facilities for protein and nucleic acid structural analysis. Ongoing research uses a variety of organisms, from bacteria to animal cells.

customFields.externalAdmissionsInformation:
The Department of Biochemistry welcomes graduate applications from individuals with a broad range of life experiences, perspectives, and backgrounds who would contribute to our community of scholars. The review process is holistic and individualized, considering each applicant’s academic record and accomplishments, letters of recommendation, prior research experience, and admissions essays to understand how an applicant’s life experiences have shaped their past and potential contributions to their field and how they might enrich the learning community at Stanford.

The Department of Biochemistry recognizes that the Supreme Court issued a ruling in June 2023 about the consideration of certain types of demographic information as part of an admission review. All applications submitted during upcoming application cycles will be reviewed in conformance with that decision.

The Stanford Biosciences Admissions Office, not the Department of Biochemistry, processes applications for the Ph.D. program. Information on how to apply for graduate study at Stanford is available on the university’s  Graduate Admissions website. All materials should be uploaded electronically to the online application.

For Autumn 2027-2028: Admissions Timeline

  • Application Opens: Mid-September 2026

  • Application Deadline: Please check the Biosciences's Admissions page for more information here.

  • Interview Session (in-person): March 3 through March 6, 2027

Those applying for graduate study should have at least a baccalaureate degree and complete work in cell and developmental biology, basic biochemistry and molecular biology, and genetics. Also required are: at least one year of university physics; differential and integral calculus; and organic, inorganic, and physical chemistry. The department is especially interested in applicants with research experience in biology or chemistry. All applicants are urged to compete for non-Stanford fellowships or scholarships, and U.S. citizens should complete an application for a National Science Foundation Predoctoral Traineeship.

Postdoctoral research training is available to graduates with a PhD or an MD degree. Qualified individuals may write to individual faculty members for further information.

rules.name: Requirements Overview
rules.description:
Students graduating with a PhD in Biochemistry from Stanford are expected to be generally proficient in core scientific areas relevant to biochemical research and the specific scientific areas most relevant to their particular thesis projects. The four core proficiency areas are:

  • Biochemistry and Biophysics

  • Quantitative and Computational Techniques

  • Genetics

  • Cell Biology

Proficiency can be demonstrated by successfully completing three full quarter graduate-level courses out of these four areas or by other means with the permission of the graduate advisor. Each quarter course can be replaced by two mini-courses.

In addition to the requirement for a PhD dissertation based on original research, students must complete advanced courses in biochemistry and related areas in their first year as part of the 135 total units required for the Ph.D. We enthusiastically recommend elective courses based on scientific interests.

For students enrolled in both the Biochemistry MS and the Biochemistry PhD programs, the Department will allow up to the University limit of 45 units of graduate level course work from the MS to apply towards the degree requirements for the PhD.

An additional requirement involves the submission of two research proposals. The student presents these proposals to a small committee of departmental faculty members responsible for monitoring the progress of student curricular and research programs and a journal club presentation. All PhD students must participate actively in the department’s seminar program. Students are encouraged to attend and present papers at regional and national meetings in cellular biochemistry and molecular biology.

Teaching experience is an integral part of the PhD curriculum and is required for the degree. Students must notify the Student Services Administrator.

The Department of Biochemistry offers an MS only to students already enrolled in the PhD program. Students should contact the Graduate Studies advisor for more details.

rules.name: Research Rotations
rules.description: First rotation must be in the Biochemistry Department. Length of rotation is flexible. Choose a lab at the end of first year, preferably by the end of spring quarter. First year students should be enrolling in BIOC 399 under Biochemistry's Graduate Advisor for all their rotations. Once a student has committed to a lab, the student should sign up for the "Graduate Research" course under their advisor; i.e., if a student committed to a lab under an advisor in Chemical and Systems Biology, the student must sign up for CSB 399 "Graduate Research" under the advisor.
