rows.name: Internatio
rows.catalogDescription: Join our interdisciplinary program devoted to rigorous analysis of international policy issues in diplomacy, governance, cyber and international security, global health, and environmental policy. Learn to integrate perspectives from political science, law, economics, history, and other disciplines, conduct original research, and implement solutions addressing global problems.

customFields.A3i6E:
The Ford Dorsey Master’s in International Policy (MIP) is an interdisciplinary program devoted to rigorously analyzing international policy issues in diplomacy, governance, cyber and international security, and environmental policy. The two-year, full-time degree program awards the Master of Arts (MA) in International Policy. 

Unique for small, collaborative classes led by top Stanford faculty and seasoned practitioners, MIP’s core curriculum emphasizes political science, economics, and international relations with quantitative methods and a case study approach. The curriculum includes a strong practical component, customization, and several subplans corresponding to expertise at the Freeman Spogli Institute for International Studies at Stanford (FSI).

In keeping with the university’s mission, MIP was established in 1982 to prepare the next generation of leaders for public and private sector careers in international policy-making and implementation. Its curriculum effectively draws upon FSI’s world-class faculty and interdisciplinary culture, breadth of teaching across theory and practice, multidisciplinary research capacity, and Stanford and Silicon Valley’s ethos of innovation. The program offers its master’s students a unique education to examine, understand, and solve complex real-world problems.

Graduate Degrees describes the university requirements for the MA degree.
customFields.WOZxr: Per university policy, students enrolled in this MA program may not apply external credits toward their degree requirements. The university’s general requirements, applicable to all graduate degrees at Stanford, are listed in Graduate Degrees.
customFields.ItCSB:
The purpose of the master’s program is to help students develop content knowledge, quantitative, analytical, and implementation skills, communication skills, and interpersonal skills in preparation for professional careers in international policy and related fields. This is achieved through completing fundamental required courses in the core curriculum and subplan, elective courses in primary and associated areas, and capstone courses. Students are also encouraged to gain professional experience through a summer internship and research skills through assistantships with Stanford faculty.

Graduates with the Master of Arts in International Policy will demonstrate an advanced understanding of international issues about governance, security, diplomacy, AI, technology, and other related areas. They will have in-depth knowledge in interpreting and analyzing qualitative and quantitative data. They will have also benefited from experiential learning that enables them to apply their theoretical knowledge, technical expertise, and policy skills in practical settings.
customFields.advisingExpectations:
The Master of Arts in International Policy (MIP) program is committed to providing comprehensive academic advising that supports students' scholarly, professional, and personal development. Effective advising is a collaborative, ongoing partnership between advisors and students, built on regular communication, mutual respect, professionalism, and integrity. Students are expected to actively engage in the advising process by seeking guidance, preparing for advising meetings, and taking responsibility for understanding university policies and MIP degree requirements.

Each MIP student is assigned three advisors: a faculty advisor, a program advisor, and a career advisor.

The faculty advisor, assigned during Autumn Quarter of the student's first year based on the student's academic interests and subplan, provides guidance on substantive matters, intellectual exploration, and professional development. Students are expected to meet with their faculty advisor at least once each quarter and are responsible for scheduling these meetings. Faculty advisors also help students navigate Stanford's academic resources, identify opportunities aligned with their interests, and connect with other faculty members whose expertise supports their academic and career goals. Students are encouraged to build relationships with faculty beyond their assigned advisor.

The program advisor (the MIP Assistant Director for Academic and Student Services) advises all students on degree requirements, academic planning and progress, university and program policies, enrollment planning, and other academic or personal matters affecting student success.

The career advisor (the MIP Career Development and Alumni Engagement Manager) provides guidance on internships, career skillbuilding and planning, professional development, and alumni engagement.

The MIP Assistant Director for Academic and Student Services and the MIP Program Coordinator monitor students' academic progress and completion of program requirements and milestones. Students are responsible for tracking their degree progress through My Academic Path (MAP) and completing all required program milestones.

Students must submit the MIP Program Proposal during Spring Quarter of their first year of enrollment. (This deadline differs from the general university policy.) The Program Proposal is a required departmental milestone that establishes the student's program of study and demonstrates how degree requirements will be satisfied.

Students must also submit the MIP Graduation Program Proposal no later than the quarter in which they apply to graduate. Completion and approval of this required milestone is necessary for degree conferral. 

Program proposal forms and additional advising resources are available on the MIP website.

More detailed information on advising is available in the MIP Student Handbook. Additional information on graduate student forms is included in the handbook and under Degree Requirements on this website.

The program adheres to the advising guidelines and responsibilities listed by the Office of the Vice Provost for Graduate Education (VPGE) and in Graduate Academic Policies (GAP).
customFields.cotermTransferPolicy: In this master’s program, courses taken three quarters before the first graduate quarter or later are eligible for consideration for transfer to the graduate career for Coterminal students. No courses taken before the first quarter of the sophomore year may be used to meet master’s degree requirements. Please visit the Coterminal Course Transfer webpage for additional details.
customFields.cotermAdmissions:
Coterminal Master's Program

Stanford undergraduates may apply for admission to the coterminal Master of Arts in International Policy program after earning a minimum of 120 units toward the bachelor's degree, including Advanced Placement and transfer credit, and no later than the quarter preceding the expected completion of the undergraduate degree.

The MIP program admits coterminal students for Autumn Quarter only. Applications, including all required supporting materials, must be submitted by the annual application deadline published on the MIP website. For Autumn Quarter 2027, the application deadline is January 7, 2027 (by 11:59 pm PST). 

Students must submit the Coterminal Online Application and apply during the same application cycle as external applicants. Please note that application to the MIP program is a competitive process.

Applicants must submit the following materials through Stanford's online application:

  • Statement of purpose describing relevant personal and professional background, academic interests, and career aspirations (approximately 1,000 words, single-spaced)

  • Stanford transcript

  • Two letters of recommendation from Stanford faculty or other university instructors

  • Academic writing sample in English (7–15 double-spaced pages; may be an excerpt from a longer paper)

  • Quantitative experience and AI skills summary (1 page, table or bullet-point format preferred)

  • Résumé or curriculum vitae

For university policies governing coterminal degree programs, see Coterminal Master’s Degrees.
customFields.programGradingPolicies:
Students must take the following courses for a letter grade:

  • MIP Core Courses

    • Exceptions:  INTLPOL 300A and 300S, both of which are only offered as Satisfactory/No Credit

  • MIP Capstone Courses

    • Exception: INTLPOL 310A, which is only offered as Satisfactory/No Credit

  • MIP Subplan (i.e., Area of Specialization) Required Courses

Students may apply up to 10 pass/fail units toward the Subplan Electives and Customized Electives. (Note: This is a combined total).

  • The 10-unit limit includes pass/fail courses taken at the: Graduate School of Business; School of Earth, Energy, and Environmental Science; School of Education; School of Engineering; School of Medicine; School of Sustainability; and School of Humanities and Sciences. This also includes Law School courses taken as: Mandatory Pass/Restricted Credit/Fail.

Students assigned a grade of Incomplete ("I") are subject to the MIP program's deadlines for completing outstanding coursework. These deadlines are more restrictive than the University's standard policy. The required completion schedule is as follows:

  • Autumn and winter quarters: Incomplete grades must be completed no later than June 30 of the same academic year. 

  • Spring quarter: Incomplete grades must be completed no later than August 30 of the same academic year.

  • Summer quarter: Incomplete grades must be completed no later than December 30 of the same calendar year.

Students are also responsible for coordinating the course completion with the instructor(s) and apprising the MIP Assistant Director for Academic and Student Affairs of progress.

Students who accrue three or more grades of Incomplete ("I") or who carry Incomplete grades over multiple academic quarters will be placed on academic probation. An exception may be granted when the student's circumstances are attributable to documented personal or medical reasons.  Documentation must be provided by Counseling and Psychological Services (CAPS), the Office of Accessible Education (OAE), or Vaden Health Center.
customFields.programGPARequirement:
To remain in good academic standing and to be eligible for the conferral of the MA degree, MIP students must maintain a minimum cumulative GPA of 3.0. Students who fail to maintain good academic standing, whether by falling below the minimum cumulative GPA of 3.0 or by failing to make satisfactory progress toward the degree, will be placed on academic probation. Continued failure to meet academic standards may result in dismissal from the University. Students experiencing academic difficulties are strongly encouraged to consult with the MIP Assistant Director for Academic and Student Affairs as early as possible to discuss available support and strategies for returning to good academic standing.

Please review the details on Minimum Progress Requirements for Graduate Students.
customFields.programAdditionalPolicies:
Courses numbered below 100 may not be applied toward graduate degree requirements. A maximum of 12 undergraduate-level units (generally numbered 100-199, with the exception of History and Political Science courses numbered 100-299) may be taken toward the INPOL-MA

Activity courses (e.g., tennis and weightlifting), performance and visual arts courses (e.g., piano, studio arts, and dance), WELLNESS courses, and other courses numbered below 100 do not satisfy MIP degree requirements. Restrictions on English proficiency courses are described in English Proficiency Courses below.

Language Courses

Units earned in language courses may be applied only toward the Customized Electives requirement. Language courses numbered below 100 do not count toward MIP degree requirements, per University policy. Students seeking advanced language study should consult the Stanford Language Center regarding available graduate-level options, including enrollment in courses numbered 395, where appropriate.

English proficiency courses for international students do not count toward MIP degree requirements.

Students planning to apply language course units toward the MA degree must obtain approval from the MIP Assistant Director for Academic and Student Affairs before the Final Study List deadline for the applicable quarter.

Directed Readings

A directed reading is an independent study conducted under the guidance and supervision of a Stanford instructor. Additional information is available in Stanford Navigator, the Stanford Bulletin, and the MIP website.

Students may propose a directed reading to satisfy subplan or Customized Electives requirements when existing course offerings do not adequately support their academic or research objectives.

Directed Reading Limits

The following restrictions apply to directed reading courses:

  • A maximum of 15 units of directed reading may be applied toward the MA degree.

  • Of these, no more than 10 units may be applied toward subplan requirements.

  • Any remaining directed reading units may be applied toward the Customized Electives requirement, subject to the 15-unit maximum.

  • Students may enroll in a maximum of 5 units per directed reading course.

  • All directed reading courses must be taken for a letter grade.

Proposal and Approval Process

Students must submit a MIP Directed Reading Proposal to the MIP Assistant Director for Academic and Student Affairs for approval. The proposal must include:

  • The proposed topic of study

  • A research or study plan

  • Course requirements, including assignments and other deliverables

  • Confirmation from the instructor (provided via signature or email confirmation)

Proposals must be submitted no later than the second Friday of the academic quarter in which the student intends to enroll. MIP will review each proposal and notify the student of its decision no later than two days before the Final Study List deadline.

If a proposal is approved, MIP will create a section of INTLPOL 299: Directed Reading for the supervising instructor. Students will enroll in the section corresponding to their instructor (e.g., INTLPOL 299-02: Directed Reading (Stoner, Kathryn)).
customFields.externalAdmissionsInformation:
Applicants should refer to the Office of Graduate Admissions website for information about graduate admission and the application process. Applications for Autumn Quarter 2027 enrollment, including all required supporting materials, must be submitted by 11:59 p.m. PST on January 7, 2027.

Applicants seeking admission to both the Master of Arts in International Policy (MIP) program and the Knight-Hennessy Scholars (KHS) program must submit separate applications to each program. For applicants to KHS, the application deadlines are:

  • Knight-Hennessy Scholars: 1:00 p.m. PDT on October 6, 2026

  • MIP: 11:59 p.m. PST on December 1, 2026

The December 1 MIP application deadline applies only to applicants seeking consideration for Knight-Hennessy Scholars.

Prerequisite Coursework

The MIP program includes a quantitatively rigorous core curriculum. Prior to enrollment, students must complete university-level introductory coursework in both microeconomics and macroeconomics through an accredited institution or an approved online course. Familiarity with calculus and introductory statistics is also recommended to prepare for the Research Methods sequence.

Detailed prerequisite course content is available in the Frequently Asked Questions on the MIP website. All prerequisite coursework must be completed before classes begin in late September but does not need to be completed before submitting an application.

Application Materials

Applicants must submit the following materials through Stanford's web-based application:

  • Statement of purpose describing relevant personal and professional background, academic interests, and career aspirations (approximately 1,000 words, single-spaced)

  • Transcripts from all institutions attended for one academic year or longer

  • Three letters of recommendation from academic and/or professional references who can evaluate the applicant's academic ability, professional accomplishments, and preparedness for graduate study

  • Academic writing sample in English (7–15 double-spaced pages; may be an excerpt from a longer paper)

  • Quantitative experience and AI skills summary (1 page, table or bullet-point format preferred)

  • Résumé or curriculum vitae

GRE scores are neither required nor considered in the admissions process.

For the purposes of application review, Stanford accepts self-submitted transcripts. Applicants should upload a scanned copy of an official transcript whenever possible. Applicants who accept an offer of admission must submit final official transcripts and degree conferral documents before enrollment. Refer to Graduate Admissions for additional information.

English Proficiency

Applicants are not required to submit English proficiency test scores if they meet one or more of the following criteria:

  • They are U.S. citizens or permanent residents.

  • Their first language is English.

  • They earned a bachelor's, master's, or doctoral degree from an institution where English was the language of instruction.

  • They have completed at least two consecutive years of professional or educational experience conducted in English within the past 10 years.

Applicants who do not meet one of these criteria must submit official scores from either the TOEFL or IELTS. The minimum TOEFL score is 100, with a minimum score of 25 in each section. The minimum IELTS score is 7. Competitive applicants typically present stronger scores.

The ETS institutional code for Stanford University is 4704.

Minimum Education Requirements

Applicants must hold, or expect to hold before enrolling at Stanford, a U.S. bachelor's degree or its international equivalent from a college or university of recognized standing. Applicants who earned their qualifying degree outside the United States should consult Stanford's degree equivalency tool to determine eligibility.

Prospective applicants are encouraged to review the Admissions section and Frequently Asked Questions on the MIP website before submitting an application.
customFields.internalAdmissionsInformation:
Current Stanford students may be eligible to apply for admission to the Master of Arts in International Policy as part of a dual degree program, subject to the policies and eligibility requirements of the participating programs.

Admission to the MIP program is competitive and requires submission of the appropriate application and supporting materials by the published annual application deadline. Students must satisfy the admission requirements of the MIP program in addition to any requirements established by the companion program. Admission decisions are made independently by each program.

Current Stanford students are encouraged to consult with the appropriate program advisors early in their academic careers to determine eligibility, develop an appropriate course of study, and understand the application process and degree requirements. Applicants should refer to the MIP website for current application procedures and deadlines.

The MIP program highlights two dual degrees that are routinely pursued. See further information on academic policies for these dual degree programs below:

Master of Business Administration and Master of Arts in International Policy (MBA/MA)

Students may pursue a dual Master of Business Administration (MBA) through the Stanford Graduate School of Business (GSB) and Master of Arts in International Policy (MA). The program is designed for students interested in careers at the intersection of business, government, and international affairs.

Prospective students may apply concurrently to the GSB and the MIP program. Separate applications must be submitted to each program, and applicants must satisfy the admission requirements of both schools. Admission decisions are made independently by each program.

Current MBA students typically apply to the dual degree no later than the end of their first year of study. MBA students beyond the first year should consult with the MIP Assistant Director for Academic and Student Affairs regarding eligibility and application procedures. Information about the dual degree and application procedures is available on the MIP website. 

Current MIP students may apply to the GSB according to the admissions deadlines and procedures established by the GSB.

Master of Science in Environment and Resources and Master of Arts in International Policy (MS/MA)

Students may pursue a dual Master of Science in Environment and Resources (MS) through the Emmett Interdisciplinary Program in Environment and Resources (E-IPER) and Master of Arts in International Policy (MA). The dual degree enables students to combine professional training in international policy with interdisciplinary study of environmental science, technology, engineering, and sustainability.

Through coursework and research across Stanford, including opportunities within the Doerr School of Sustainability, students develop expertise in both public policy and the technical dimensions of environmental challenges. In accordance with university policy governing dual degrees, there is no reduction in the unit requirements for either degree.

Students interested in the dual degree must obtain approval from both MIP and E-IPER to ensure their proposed course of study satisfies the requirements of each program. MIP students are encouraged to consult with the MIP Assistant Director for Academic and Student Affairs and the E-IPER/SDSS Student Services Officer before applying.

First-year MIP students should apply during Winter Quarter according to the application deadline established annually by E-IPER. In exceptional circumstances, second-year MIP students may also apply. These applicants must demonstrate preparation for the MS degree by completing, or being enrolled in, at least nine units of E-IPER-related coursework at the time of application. Completion of this minimum coursework does not guarantee admission.

Application information is available on the E-IPER website.

The Master of Arts in International Policy (MIP) offers joint degree opportunities with selected Stanford graduate programs, enabling students to integrate the study of international policy with complementary professional disciplines. Joint degree programs provide an interdisciplinary course of study while allowing students to satisfy the degree requirements of both participating programs.

Admission to each joint degree program requires separate approval by both participating programs. Applicants must meet the admission requirements and academic policies established by each program. Students should consult the MIP website and the participating school's website for current application procedures, eligibility requirements, and deadlines.

Juris Doctor and Master of Arts in International Policy (JD/MA)

Students may pursue a joint Juris Doctor (JD) and Master of Arts in International Policy (MA), combining the strengths of Stanford Law School and the Master of Arts in International Policy program.

Prospective students may apply concurrently to the Stanford Law School (SLS) and MIP program. Separate applications must be submitted to each program, and applicants must satisfy the admission requirements of both schools. Information about the joint degree and application procedures is available on the Stanford Law School and MIP websites.

Current Stanford Law School students may apply to the joint degree program no later than the end of their second year of law school. Current MIP students may apply to Stanford Law School according to the deadlines and procedures established by SLS.

MIP has one annual application deadline on January 7, 2027. Applications are due no later than 11:59 p.m. PST.

Master of Public Policy and Master of Arts in International Policy (MPP/MA)

Students may pursue a joint Master of Public Policy (MPP) and Master of Arts in International Policy (MA) to develop expertise in both domestic and international public policy.

Admission to the joint degree requires admission to and enrollment in the MIP program, as well as admission to the Public Policy Program. Applicants must satisfy the admission requirements of both programs.

External applicants interested in the joint degree should apply to the MIP program and indicate their interest in the joint MPP/MA. Applicants admitted to MIP will then be considered for admission to the MPP program.

Current MIP students may apply to the joint degree during their first or second year of study and are encouraged to consult with the MIP Assistant Director for Academic and Student Affairs regarding eligibility and application procedures.

Applicants must submit all required application materials by the admission deadline established annually by the Public Policy Program. Additional information is available on the Public Policy website. See Joint Degree Programs for university policies governing joint degrees.

MIP has one annual application deadline on January 7, 2027. Applications are due no later than 11:59 p.m. PST.

See further information on academic policies for these joint degree programs below.

​​To earn the MA in International Policy, students must complete a minimum of 80 units. The degree requirements are as follows:

Core Curriculum (27 units)

All core courses are fundamental and must be completed during the first year, with the exception of INTLPOL 300S, which is required in the Winter Quarter of the second year.

  • The associated Field Research course, taken in Spring Quarter of the second year

Students who matriculated prior to Autumn Quarter 2026 should refer to the Archived Bulletins for applicable degree requirements.

The Ford Dorsey Master’s in International Policy (MIP) offers four subplans:

  • Cyber Policy and Security (CYBER)

  • Energy, Natural Resources, and the Environment (ENRE)

  • Governance and Development (GOVDEV)

  • International Security (ISEC)

Students must select one subplan and complete a minimum of five courses totaling at least 20 units. Each subplan includes two required courses that must be completed during the first year. In addition, students must complete at least three additional approved elective courses from the relevant Subplan Elective Course list.

Complete details for each subplan are provided in the individual subplan sections below.
rules.name: Subplans

rules.description:
Students must complete a minimum of 24 units of Customized Electives.

Customized Electives provide students the opportunity to engage with academic offerings across the University and tailor their course of study to their individual academic and professional interests. All courses applied toward this requirement must be broadly related to international policy.

Students may fulfill this requirement through a variety of pathways, including but not limited to: enrollment in additional subplan courses; completion of certificate programs (e.g., Computational Social Science Certificate); enrollment in language courses; completion of coursework in a second subplan (informally); or a combination of courses across disciplines that support the student’s academic objectives.

Courses numbered below 100 may not be applied toward graduate degree requirements, in accordance with University policy. In addition, activity courses, as well as performance and visual arts courses, do not satisfy MIP degree requirements.

Practical Training

Students may participate in an internship or other supervised practical experience that complements their degree program and subplan. With program approval, a maximum of 3 units of practical training may be applied toward the Customized Electives requirement.

During the academic year (Autumn, Winter, and Spring Quarters), students enroll in the designated Practical Training course (INTLPOL 298: Practical Training). A separate Practical Training course is offered during Summer Quarter (INTLPOL 298S: Practical Training). Both courses satisfy the academic enrollment requirement for Curricular Practical Training (CPT) for eligible students in F-1 status.

Students requesting enrollment in a Practical Training course for CPT purposes must submit the MIP CPT Proposal by the second Friday of the academic quarter in which they intend to enroll. 

Additional information regarding eligibility, enrollment procedures, and CPT requirements is available on the MIP website and in the MIP Student Handbook.
rules.name: Customized Electives

rules.description:
The Policy Change Studio serves as the capstone experience for the MIP program. In this fundamental course, student teams work under faculty supervision with external partners from industry, government, and the nonprofit sector to address complex policy challenges. The capstone is project-based and emphasizes the development of feasible, implementation-oriented solutions for real-world clients.

Course Enrollment Requirements

Students enroll in the Policy Change Studio over Winter Quarter and Spring Quarter of the second year, for a total of 8 units.

In addition, students enroll in the associated field research component course during Spring Quarter of the second year.

The MIP Capstone is a fundamental component of the degree program and exceptions are not permitted under any circumstances.

requisitesSimple.notes:
Program Proposal

Students must submit a MIP Master's Degree Program Proposal during the Spring Quarter of their first year of study. As part of this requirement, students must schedule a 30-minute advising appointment with the MIP Academic Services Team to review their academic progress and develop a plan for completing the remaining degree requirements.

The University requires all graduate students to have an approved program proposal on file with their degree program. Students who do not complete this requirement will have an enrollment hold placed on their student account until the requirement has been satisfied. 

Please see the Graduate Advising page for additional details.

Graduation Program Proposal

Students must submit a  MIP Graduate Program Proposal in the quarter in which they intend to graduate, or no later than the second week of the intended graduation quarter. This proposal serves as formal confirmation of the student’s academic plan and degree completion status.

Failure to submit the required Graduation Program Proposal by the stated deadline will result in denial of the application to graduate.

rules.description:
Subplan Requirements

Students must select one subplan and complete a minimum of five courses within that subplan, totaling at least 20 units. Each subplan includes two required courses, which must be completed during the first year of study. In addition, students must complete at least three approved subplan elective courses, selected from the subplan elective course list.

The list of approved subplan elective courses is available below and on the MIP website.

Subplan Selection

Upon matriculation, students will see their assigned subplan reflected in Axess based on the selection submitted at the time of admission. Students will be asked to confirm or update their subplan prior to matriculation in Autumn Quarter; this designation is used to assign faculty advisors.

Students may request to change their subplan through the end of the first academic year, subject to approval by the MIP Assistant Director for Academic and Student Affairs.

Approved subplan changes must be processed through the Declaration or Change to a Field of Study for Graduate Students (Subplan Change) eForm in Axess.

Subplan Course Planning

Required subplan courses must be completed during the first year of study unless an exception is approved due to unavoidable scheduling conflicts. Approval to defer a required subplan course to the second year must be granted in advance by the MIP Assistant Director for Academic and Student Affairs.

No exemptions are permitted for required subplan courses. Coterminal students who have previously completed a required subplan course as part of their undergraduate program should consult with MIP regarding alternative course options to avoid duplication.

All required subplan courses must be taken for a letter grade. A limited number of subplan elective courses may be taken on a pass/fail basis, subject to University and MIP program grading policies. Courses numbered below 100 may not be applied toward graduate degree requirements.

Subplan Course Petition Process

Twice per year, MIP accepts petitions to add courses to the list of approved subplan electives. This process allows students to propose courses for review by MIP leadership and faculty subject-matter leads for the relevant subplan.

Petition submission timelines will be announced in advance of each review cycle. Students must submit complete course information, including a syllabus and a written rationale for inclusion.

Course review criteria include:

  • Alignment with subplan learning objectives

  • Student-provided rationale for inclusion

  • Recency and consistency of course offerings

  • Graduate-level designation (generally courses numbered 200 and above)

  • Availability of a letter grade option (except in GSB, Law, and School of Medicine courses where applicable)

  • Teaching evaluations, when available

Skills-based or primarily experiential courses are typically classified as Customized Electives rather than subplan electives.

Approved courses will be added to the official subplan elective list. Students may apply a course retroactively toward subplan requirements if it is approved after the course has been completed.

The elective course list includes both currently offered and historically approved courses, maintained as part of the program record in accordance with University policy. A current list of active courses is available on the MIP website.

requisitesSimple.notes:
Stanford MIP-Vienna School of International Studies Academic Exchange

The Stanford MIP–Vienna School of International Studies Academic Exchange is a one-quarter (Autumn Quarter) exchange program between the Ford Dorsey Master’s in International Policy (MIP) and the Diplomatische Akademie Wien – Vienna School of International Studies (DA). Each year, two second-year students from each institution are selected through a competitive application process to participate in the exchange. Selected students receive fellowships to study at the partner institution, where they enroll as full-time students, participate in academic and extracurricular activities, and engage in the intellectual community of the host institution.

Academic Policies

Students participating in the exchange must complete all requirements of the MIP MA curriculum. The minimum number of Stanford units required for graduation is reduced to 65 units for students participating in the exchange.

In addition to the Stanford unit requirement, students must complete the equivalent of at least 15 units (typically four or more full-time courses) at the Vienna School of International Studies.  These courses will apply towards the subplan electives or Customized Electives.  As such, the two required subplan courses must be completed at Stanford.

MIP exchange participants must submit their proposed DA course selections to the MIP Academic Services Team for approval no later than the end of the first week of classes in the Autumn Trimester at the DA.

Students are strongly encouraged to carefully evaluate how coursework completed at the DA will apply toward MIP degree requirements and to consider the implications of spending one quarter away from Stanford. 

Enrollment and Transcript Policy

While participating in the exchange, students remain active in their Stanford academic program; however, they are not considered enrolled at Stanford during the exchange quarter. Students receive an official transcript from the Vienna School of International Studies for the Autumn Trimester. The exchange is not reflected on the Stanford transcript.

Additional Information

Further details are available on the Stanford–Vienna Academic Exchange page of the MIP website.

requisitesSimple.name: Narrative Text
requisitesSimple.notes:
Allocation of Credit for Dual Degree Programs involving the Master of Arts in International Policy

Dual Degree: GSB-MBA/INPOL-MA

The dual MBA/MA program is typically completed in approximately three academic years, depending on prior academic preparation and quantitative background.

Admissions decisions are made independently by each program. Units may not be double-counted toward both degrees; coursework must be applied to either the MBA or the MA degree requirements, but not both.

Students in the dual degree program must complete:

  • 90 units for the MBA

  • 54 units for the MA in International Policy, including the following requirements: 

  • Core curriculum: 27 units

  • Subplan: 18 units

  • Capstone: 9 units 

Students should consult both the MBA Program Office and the MIP Assistant Director for Academic and Student Affairs for additional guidance.

Dual Degree: ENVRES-MS/INPOL-MA

Students must complete all degree requirements for both programs, including 80 units for the MA in International Policy and 45 units for the MS in Environment and Resources. Completing the MS degree typically requires at least three additional quarters of study beyond the time required to complete the MA.

Joint Degree: LAW-JD/INPOL-MA

The joint JD requires 111 units, and the MA in International Policy requires 54 units. Students enrolled in the joint program must complete the following MIP requirements:

  • Core curriculum: 27 units

  • Subplan 18 units

  • Capstone 9 units 

Students who begin their studies at Stanford Law School may, with MIP approval, complete the required statistics sequence through the Law School in place of the INTLPOL statistics sequence. However, this option is not recommended, as the Law School sequence typically includes a single statistics course, whereas the INTLPOL sequence consists of two courses that provide broader methodological preparation (including training in R) for the MIP capstone. 

Students who elect this option may be at a disadvantage in capstone preparation. Prior approval from MIP is required. Any resulting unit adjustments will be applied to subplan requirements as appropriate.

In addition, Customized Electives are not required for joint JD students who matriculate first in the Law School. In some cases, Customized Electives may also be waived for students who matriculate first in MIP, subject to program approval.

Joint Degree: MPP/INPOL-MA

The MPP requires 90 units, and the MA in International Policy requires 80 units. In approved joint degree programs, up to 45 units (or one year of residency) may be applied toward both degrees. As a result, the total unit requirement for the joint degree may be reduced by up to 45 units compared to the combined requirements of the two individual degrees.

The MPP/MA joint degree program requires a three-year residency, reflecting this overlap in coursework and program requirements.

The Public Policy Program encourages the development of a strong intellectual, professional, and social cohort experience. For this reason, joint degree students are strongly encouraged to complete one academic year of full-time study dedicated exclusively to the Public Policy Program, rather than distributing Public Policy coursework across multiple years of study.

Coterminal Master's Degree Requirements

Coterminal students admitted to MIP must complete the following requirements to earn the MA in International Policy:

  • Core curriculum: 27 units

  • Subplan: 20 units, including:

rows.name: JEWSH-BA
rows.catalogDescription: This program provides you with an understanding of Jewish history, language, literature, religion, thought, and politics to help you understand Jewish identity, thought, and self-expression within larger historical and social contexts and to develop your ability to analyze human experience from different disciplinary perspectives.

customFields.A3i6E:
The Jewish Studies major provides students with an overview of Jewish history, languages, literature, religion, thought, and politics. Drawing from the Humanities, the Social Sciences, and from courses offered by affiliated faculty in the School of Education, the Jewish Studies major seeks to help students understand Jewish identities, thought, and culture within larger historical and social contexts and to develop their ability to analyze human experience from a variety of disciplinary perspectives. Students can explore the multiplicity of racial, ethnic, and religious meanings claimed by or assigned to Jews historically and today.

In addition to the undergraduate major and minor offered through the Interdepartmental Program in CSRE, the Taube Center for Jewish Studies offers a full range of guest lectures, conferences, and symposia. 

The Interdepartmental Program in Comparative Studies in Race and Ethnicity (CSRE) explores how race and ethnicity shape global history, undergird our social systems, and touch every aspect of our lives. Our courses empower students with the tools to assess and build inclusivity, equity, diversity, accessibility, and justice. CCSRE programs—encompassing Asian American Studies, Chicana/o-Latina/o Studies, Comparative Studies in Race and Ethnicity, Jewish Studies, and Native American Studies—take an interdisciplinary approach to considering how gender, sexuality, ability, capital, technology, education, politics, and the environment structure our bodies, experiences, and communities. Students have the option to focus on particular racial and ethnic groups and on issues that move across peoples and places. 

The interdisciplinary nature of the academic programs empowers students to enroll in a wide variety of courses. CCSRE listings can be found in Anthropology, Art and Art History, Education, History, Linguistics, Literature, Music, Philosophy, Political Science, Psychology, Religious Studies, Sociology, Theater and Performance Studies, and more. Majors and minors in CCSRE engage with various perspectives and methodologies and grapple with pivotal themes, including decolonization, indigeneity, intersectionality, movement-building, resistance, solidarity, and wellness. By analyzing interlocking structures of identity and difference, CCSRE students interrogate the role of power, reimagine the world, and reclaim the future.
customFields.WOZxr: Up to 20 units of external credit may be applied toward elective coursework in the major.
customFields.ItCSB:
The Program in Jewish Studies expects that undergraduate majors concluding their course of study will be able to:

  • Demonstrate broad knowledge of Jewish history (ancient through contemporary), texts, and religion while specializing in a disciplinary approach to the study of Jews, Judaism, and Jewish cultures

  • Mobilize comparative frameworks for analyzing how race, ethnicity, and religion develop historically, cross-culturally, and transnationally with a focus on Jewish racialization

  • Understand, interpret, and utilize trans- and interdisciplinary theories and methods in the study of race, ethnicity, and religion as they pertain to Jews

  • Critically engage with primary and secondary sources and use both types of evidence in research and argumentation, including demonstrating the ability to engage with a Jewish language

  • Effectively communicate data, research, and arguments to diverse audiences

  • Apply a core inventory of theories, methods, and concepts to local and global contexts

rows.name: LAMER-MA
rows.catalogDescription: This interdisciplinary program consists of a core set of courses surveying the Latin American region’s history, politics, society, ecology, and culture; advanced language training; and in-depth coursework. You’ll choose a course of study suited to your interests.

customFields.A3i6E:
The Master of Arts in Latin American Studies is an interdisciplinary program designed to develop students' knowledge and skills in the study of Latin America and to prepare them for professional careers or doctoral study.

The curriculum comprises courses surveying the region, including its history, politics, society, ecology, and culture; advanced language training; research methodology; and focused coursework within the program's three fields of specialization (humanities, environment and health, and social sciences). In consultation with their faculty advisor(s), students select a course of study suited to their interests. Students with little prior coursework in Latin American Studies may benefit most from this interdisciplinary approach.

Graduates of the program have entered a range of fields, including higher education, business, the private sector, government, and nonprofit organizations.
customFields.WOZxr: The program does not accept external credit.
customFields.ItCSB:
Upon completion of the Master of Arts in Latin American Studies, students will be able to:

  1. Demonstrate interdisciplinary knowledge of Latin America's history, politics, society, culture, and environment, drawing connections across disciplines to analyze regional issues.

  2. Apply advanced disciplinary expertise within a chosen field of specialization (humanities, environment and health, or social sciences) to a focused area of inquiry.

  3. Communicate effectively in a relevant language of the region (such as Spanish, Portuguese, Quechua, Nahuatl, or Haitian Creole) at an advanced level, enabling engagement with primary sources and communities.

  4. Conduct independent research by designing and completing a capstone or thesis project that culminates in a substantial written work, under the guidance of a faculty advisor.

  5. Learn about diverse research methods, systems, and tools to investigate and present findings on Latin American topics.

  6. Critically evaluate scholarship and sources on Latin America, synthesizing diverse perspectives to construct well-supported arguments.

  7. Prepare for professional or academic pathways by developing the analytical, linguistic, and methodological skills relevant to careers in higher education, government, business, the private sector, and nonprofit organizations, among others, or to doctoral study.
customFields.advisingExpectations:
The Center for Latin American Studies (CLAS) is committed to providing academic advising in support of graduate students' scholarly and professional development. At its most effective, this advising relationship entails collaborative and sustained engagement between the advisor and the advisee. As a best practice, advising expectations should be periodically discussed and reviewed to ensure mutual understanding, and both parties are expected to maintain professionalism and integrity.

Advising Roles

Faculty advisors guide students in critical areas such as selecting courses, designing and conducting research, and exploring academic opportunities and professional pathways. The CLAS director of graduate studies (DGS) provides academic advising and overall intellectual guidance to Latin American Studies MA students; the DGS serves in a secondary role to the assigned faculty advisor and may act as a second reader of MA theses and capstone papers. Program administrative staff advise students on program policies, degree requirements, and course selection. The CLAS academic and student services officer informs students and advisors about University and department requirements, procedures, and opportunities, and maintains the official records of advising assignments and approvals.

Student Responsibilities

Graduate students are active contributors to the advising relationship. They should proactively seek academic and professional guidance, take responsibility for informing themselves of the policies and degree requirements for their program, and remain aware of all program-specific and University-wide deadlines.

Advisor Assignments

At the start of graduate study, generally during autumn quarter, each student is assigned a faculty advisor—a member of the program's faculty who provides research advice and guidance in course selection and in exploring academic opportunities and professional pathways. At least one faculty advisor per student must be a member of the Stanford Academic Council. Usually, the same faculty member serves as the program advisor for the duration of the master's study; however, formal advisor change requests may be made in consultation with CLAS staff.

Meeting Expectations

Students should meet with their advisors at least once per quarter to discuss the courses they plan to take and to seek their advisors' input and guidance. In addition, MA students must participate in the CLAS MA quarterly meetings, held during the second half of each quarter. The CLAS director, director of graduate studies, associate director, and student services officer meet with all students during these mandatory meetings and are available by email and during office hours throughout the academic year.

Additional Resources

See the Graduate Academic Policies and Procedures handbook and the University Bulletin's Graduate Advising section for the University policy statements on graduate advising. Academic advising by Stanford faculty is a critical component of every graduate student's education; additional resources can be found in the Policies & Practices for Advising Relationships guide and the Guidelines for Advising Relationships Between Faculty and Graduate Students.

Students who wish to undertake a more intensive program of study, including independent research, should pursue departmental honors. subRules.name: Requirements Overview
subRules.description:
Individual programs should be worked out in advance with an advisor in Linguistics, keeping the above requirements in mind.

Program Requirements Overview

  • The MA degree requires the completion of 45 units, at least 36 of these must be in Linguistics.

  • The coursework must include five basic courses as described in the Course Requirements section; these courses must be completed with at least a B and taken for four units.

  • The overall coursework grade point average (GPA) must be at least 3.0 (B). A GPA of less than 3.0 indicates that a student may not be performing at the level expected of an MA student in the program.

  • At least 30 units taken towards the 45 units of degree program coursework must be taken for a letter grade.

  • No more than two courses should be at the 100 level and no course should be below the 100 level.

  • If the student can make a compelling case, the department may allow up to 9 of the 45 units to be in a department other than Linguistics. Courses from outside the department must have explicit linguistic content; furthermore, if the student is simultaneously enrolled in a degree program in another department, not all of these 9 units can be earned in that department.

Course Requirements Overview

  • The basic breadth courses are divided into Groups I and II, which in turn are divided into subgroups, e.g., Phonetics and Phonology, Morphology, Computational Linguistics, etc.

  • Students are required to take a total of five courses from Groups I and II.

  • The courses must be from 4 different subgroups, at least from 1 subgroup within Group I and from 1 subgroup within Group II.

  • The fifth course must be drawn from one of these 4 subgroups, providing more depth in one subgroup.

  • Students may take more courses in any given subgroup as additional courses.

  • One further course providing exposure to current research in a subfield of linguistics (1 unit, S/NC); see the Linguistics MA Program Proposal form for the current list.

rows.name: Law (JD)
rows.catalogDescription: Experience our innovative approach to a truly interdisciplinary, multidimensional legal education through which you’ll learn to think not just like lawyers but also like clients and scholars. You’ll encounter diverse learning opportunities, benefit from academic thought leaders in law and across disciplines, and enjoy the intellectual life of the campus.

customFields.A3i6E:
Mastering legal doctrine is just the beginning of a proper legal education. Lawyers play countless roles in our society—as advocates, as advisors, as leaders in their own right. They practice law, work in business and government, put their degrees to use in science, education, and policymaking, and serve their communities in many other ways. Knowledge of the law, both its content and how to argue about it, remains critical in all these roles. But it is not enough, and a lawyer must also understand the needs of the people he or she serves and the consequences for them of different legal positions. And because those needs cross disciplinary boundaries, Stanford Law—true to Stanford University’s heritage of learning without limits—offers the opportunity for a truly interdisciplinary, multidimensional legal education.

Stanford Law has adopted a variety of innovative approaches to prepare students to think not just like lawyers but also like clients and scholars. To begin, we make it easy to experience the diverse learning opportunities that are possible only at a university like Stanford—with its breadth of highly ranked schools and departments, all located close together on a well connected physical campus. Stanford Law students have broad access to courses outside the law school that will fill out their legal education. In this way, students benefit from academic thought leaders across disciplines, not to mention the intellectual life of the campus found in the myriad of conferences and events held each year and in countless other multidisciplinary research programs.

Nor do the opportunities to broaden your legal education at Stanford Law end here. In addition, you can explore law’s intersection with a growing range of fields by pursuing a joint degree and adding a master’s or doctorate to your law degree or by taking teamwork oriented simulation courses with students and faculty from other parts of the university.

See the Law School website for further information about admission, programs, curriculum, and faculty.
customFields.ItCSB:
The ABA requires each law school to “establish and publish learning outcomes” designed to “prepare its students, upon graduation, for admission to the bar and for effective, ethical, and responsible participation as members of the profession.” ABA Standards 301 (a) & (b). The syllabus for each course may either set forth the course’s particular Learning Outcomes or direct students to the online course description, where Learning Outcomes are provided. By completing your degree, Stanford Law School certifies that you have satisfied the ABA’s Learning Outcome requirements listed below.

  • LO1: Exhibit knowledge and understanding of key concepts in substantive law, procedural law, and legal thought.

  • LO2: Demonstrate facility with legal analysis and reasoning. This may include, but will not necessarily include, a combination of skills such as synthesizing cases, identifying and applying relevant principles, and mastering modes of inquiry (whether scientific, social scientific, or humanistic) that inform and contextualize legal analysis and reasoning.

  • LO3: Demonstrate the ability to conduct legal research.

  • LO4: Demonstrate the ability to communicate effectively in writing.

  • LO5: Demonstrate the ability to communicate orally (such as in group or individual presentations, while delivering advice to a client, or in the course of oral advocacy).

  • LO6: Display familiarity with the law governing lawyers and exhibit an understanding of a lawyer’s distinctive ethical responsibilities to clients, the legal system, and the broader public.

  • LO7: Display other professional skills needed for effective and responsible participation in the legal profession (such as, interviewing; counseling; negotiation; fact development and analysis; trial practice; contract review and drafting; conflict resolution; leadership behaviors, attitudes, and styles; collaboration and teamwork; execution; and cultural competency).

In the process of completing their units, they must satisfy the following curricular requirements:

In accordance with ABA accreditation standards, JD students may not count toward the JD graduation requirement more than thirty-one (31) quarter units of the following types of coursework: externship, directed research, directed writing, senior thesis, research track, courses taken outside the Law School, moot court (Kirkwood competition), Trial Lawyer Skills Workshop, and Law Journal Discussion Group.

rules.description:
Unit Requirements

JD students must complete all first-year required courses, plus an additional 81 approved quarter units of elective coursework.

First-year JD students must abide by the following guidelines for elective credit:

  • During the Autumn Quarter, a first-year student may take only designated first-year required courses.

  • During Winter Quarter they may take no more than 5 units of electives.

  • During Spring quarter they must take 3-8 units of electives.

Elective courses are limited to those within the Law School, with the exception that first-year JD students may take a physical education course or music lessons each quarter but those courses will not count toward residency or graduation. Limited exceptions to this can be made if a course is required in the Spring Quarter for a joint degree program.

Experiential Learning Requirement

Students must complete 8 units of coursework designated as fulfilling the Experiential Learning (EL) requirement pursuant to ABA Standard 303.

Pathway A – Full-time Clinic:

Students who complete any of Stanford Law School’s full-time clinics are deemed “Pathway A” students. These students will automatically satisfy the ABA Experiential Learning Requirement.

Pathway B – Self-Design:

Students who do not enroll in one of Stanford Law School’s full-time clinics are deemed “Pathway B” students. Pathway B students must submit to the Registrar’s Office a Self-Design Plan specifying which courses the student has taken and/or intends to take to satisfy the ABA Experiential Learning Requirement and the SLS Professional Writing graduation requirement.

Courses that count towards the EL requirement are identified on the Registrar’s website and in course listings. Students choosing Pathway B to fulfill this requirement should note that not all courses are offered every year and that enrollment for some courses may be limited.

All students who elect Pathway B must include a Professional Writing (“PW”) course of at least two units within their individually tailored plan. A course designated as a “PW” course is defined as one in which the students engage in the sort of professional writing common to practicing lawyers, e.g. writing briefs, drafting contracts, etc. PW courses include only those approved by the Curriculum Committee and explicitly classified as a PW class before the term begins. Externships and courses outside the law school do not satisfy the Professional Writing requirement. Courses that are designated as both EL and PW courses can count for both requirements.

Ethics Requirement

JD students must complete at least one advanced course that contains one or more units of ethics instruction. Only a course approved by the Curriculum Committee and explicitly classified as an ethics course before the quarter begins satisfies this requirement.

Writing Requirement

In addition to first-year Legal Writing and Federal Litigation, all students must complete one course of at least two units in which a principal part of the assigned work is a paper or other written product (an “R” paper), and one course of at least two units in which a principal part of the assigned work is typical of the sort of writing done by practicing lawyers, such as writing briefs and drafting contracts (a professional Writing “PW” course). Only courses approved by the Curriculum Committee and explicitly classified as an R or a PW course before the term begins can satisfy these requirements.

  • A course designated as an “R” course is defined as one in which the written product is substantial and is based on open-ended research by the student.

  • A Directed Research paper may count as the equivalent of an “R” course with the approval of the supervising faculty member.

  • Satisfactory completion of a Senior Thesis or Research Track counts as the equivalent of an “R” course.

Double-Counting Requirements

Students cannot use a single course to satisfy the “R,” “Ethics,” and/or “Experiential Learning” requirements. If a course potentially satisfies multiple graduation requirements, then the student must choose which graduation requirement the course should be attributed to, with one exception. While typically students wishing to use a course to satisfy the Experiential Learning requirement cannot double-count that course for other graduation requirements, and must use that course solely to satisfy the Experiential Learning requirement, students may use a course designated as both an EL course and a PW course to satisfy both EL and PW requirements.

Study toward this degree is open only to exceptionally well-qualified students who hold a JD or its equivalent and who have successfully completed a U.S.-based LLM program or Stanford’s SPILS program. It is awarded to students who, under the personal supervision of a faculty member, successfully pursue a course of advanced research in a field in which they are already well grounded, and who produce an advanced dissertation that, in the opinion of the adviser, makes a substantial contribution to knowledge. Overview of Degree Requirements

The requirements for the degree of Doctor of the Science of Law are: 

  • Three quarters in residency during the first JSD year

  • Successful completion of 9 - 12 approved quarter units during the first JSD year, including at least one methodological course

  • Successful completion of an oral exam at the end of the first JSD year, intended to determine the candidate’s readiness to embark on doctoral research, as determined by the candidate’s dissertation committee chair and at least one other Stanford faculty member 

  • Filing of a Doctoral Dissertation Reading Committee Form, signed by each member of the committee, as well as the Associate Dean for Graduate Studies

  • Successful completion of an advanced dissertation, as determined by a faculty dissertation advisory committee 

  • Successful completion of an oral defense of the dissertation, as determined by the same dissertation advisory committee

  • Successful participation in the JSD colloquium during the first year and all subsequent years in which the student is in residence

  • Timely filing of an application for graduation

Unit Requirement 

To obtain a JSD degree, a student must successfully complete, under the personal supervision of a faculty member, an approved 44-unit course of study. Credits earned to meet the JSM requirements will count toward 35 of these quarter units. At least 26 of those 35 units must be in Law School courses; however, see the SLS Student Handbook for the policies and limitations on enrolling in courses from elsewhere at the university. 

Students must participate in a year-long research colloquium (0 units) designed especially for JSD students. In addition, JSD students in their first year must take three courses of at least three units each, for a minimum of 9 but no more than 15 units. No student may take more than eight units in a single quarter. 

At least one of these additional courses must provide advanced methodological training, and the remaining courses must provide further study in a substantive field related to the student’s doctoral research. All three must be approved by the student’s dissertation chair or the Associate Dean for Graduate Studies. Generally, directed research will not satisfy the coursework requirement units unless it is intended to provide the student with new or enhanced methodological, theoretical knowledge, or substantive knowledge that is essential to carrying out that student’s dissertation research and that is not offered by any regularly scheduled courses or seminars at Stanford during the candidate’s first year in the JSD program. Candidates seeking credit for directed research while in residence must petition and receive the approval of their dissertation advisor, the Associate Dean for Graduate Studies, and the Petitions Committee. 

Students in the first year of the JSD program (i.e., who have completed the JSM degree and have been admitted to the JSD program) will be entitled to terminal graduate registration (“TGR”) status, which allows students to register at a reduced tuition rate and pay for additional units.

Refer to the SLS Student Handbook for details about the JSD graduation requirements.

Residency Requirement

JSD candidates must complete a full academic year (three quarters) in residence at the Law School. This requirement is in addition to quarters in residence that may have been completed as part of the SPILS program. Thus, students who go through the SPILS program and then enter the JSD program must be in residence at Stanford Law School for six full quarters. For JSD candidates on TGR status, “in residence” means that a student is physically on campus and regularly meets with their advisor throughout the quarter.

requisitesSimple.name: Oral Exam
requisitesSimple.notes:
All JSD candidates must pass an oral examination at the end of the first academic year of the JSD program (normally before the University’s commencement date) and must successfully defend their dissertation orally at the completion of the program.

The first-year oral exam is intended to determine the candidate’s readiness to embark on doctoral research. Normally, the candidate will be asked to present plans for doctoral research (i.e., the research proposal) and will be expected to demonstrate mastery of the research literature and theoretical concepts relevant to the dissertation topic, and competence to deploy the required research methods. The candidate’s dissertation adviser will determine the exact content and format of the exam. First-year JSD candidates are encouraged to discuss with their dissertation advisers how best to prepare for the oral examination.

First year oral examinations will be given under the supervision of the faculty dissertation adviser. At least one additional Stanford faculty member will also participate in the oral examination. Candidates are encouraged to form their dissertation committee during their first year in residence and request that all members of the committee participate in the oral exam. If the candidate does not pass the oral examination, the candidate must retake the exam at a later time. Any such candidate should meet with their adviser to receive guidance concerning why their performance on the oral examination was insufficient to pass and how those deficiencies can be corrected with further preparation in advance of the second oral examination. In the event that the candidate needs to retake the oral examination, the second exam will be before a panel including at least three faculty examiners. A second failure to pass an oral examination will disqualify the student from the JSD program.

The oral dissertation defense is given under the supervision of the doctoral dissertation adviser and all members of dissertation committee. At the discretion of the dissertation chair, one member of the committee (but only one) may participate by videoconference. Oral dissertation defenses are not open to the public.

The School of Law, established in 1893, provides a legal education for students who are fit by their maturity and academic training to pursue professional study under university methods of instruction. The curriculum leading to the first professional degree in law, the Doctor of Jurisprudence (JD), constitutes an adequate preparation for law practice in any English-speaking jurisdiction. Graduate work leading to the degrees of Master of Laws (LLM), Master of the Science of Law (JSM), and Doctor of the Science of Law (JSD), and a non-professional degree, Master of Legal Studies (MLS), is also offered. For the entire curriculum, see the Course Schedule & Description on the Law School website. Stanford Law School offers joint or dual degree options with other Stanford graduate departments and universities nationwide; see Joint and Dual Degrees in Law below.

Stanford Law School offers four LLM (Master of Laws) degrees, an LLM in Corporate Governance and Practice, an LLM in Environmental Law and Policy, an LLM in International Economic Law, Business and Policy, and an LLM in Law, Science and Technology. The LLM degree is awarded only to individuals with a JD degree (or its equivalent). For complete information about the LLM programs, visit the SLS Student Handbook.

rows.catalogDescription: The Master of Legal Studies (MLS) is a nonprofessional degree designed for advanced graduate students from the United States or abroad who have no prior legal training and whose interdisciplinary research requires knowledge of the foundations of the legal system.

customFields.A3i6E:
The MLS (Master of Legal Studies) is a non-professional degree designed to introduce a small number of graduate students and scholars in other disciplines to the foundations of the legal system, the basic modes of legal argumentation and analysis, legal procedure, and the substantive law of selected areas. The MLS is intended primarily for those pursuing academic careers.

Exceptionally qualified MLS applicants may also apply to participate in the SPILS Program.
customFields.ItCSB: The Master of Legal Studies (MLS) is a nonprofessional degree designed for advanced graduate students from the United States or abroad who have no prior legal training and whose interdisciplinary research requires knowledge of the foundations of the legal system. Only a few such students, if any, are admitted in a given year. Questions concerning the MLS should be directed to graduate.admissions@law.stanford.edu.
customFields.advisingExpectations:
The Stanford Law School is committed to providing academic advising in support of graduate student scholarly and professional development. When most effective, this advising relationship entails collaborative and sustained engagement by the advisor and the advisee. As a best practice, advising expectations should be periodically discussed and reviewed to ensure mutual understanding. Both the advisor and the advisee are expected to maintain professionalism and integrity.

Faculty advisors guide students in critical areas such as selecting courses, designing and conducting research, developing teaching pedagogy, navigating policies and degree requirements, and exploring academic opportunities and professional pathways.

Graduate students are active contributors to the advising relationship, proactively seeking academic and professional guidance and taking responsibility for informing themselves of policies and degree requirements for their graduate program.

See Graduate Advising for a statement of university policy on graduate advising.
customFields.programAdditionalPolicies:
Residency Requirement

To graduate, a student must be “in residence” as a law student for at least three quarters. For purposes of the MLS degree, the term “in residence” means that a student:

  • Takes at least 9 quarter units of credit that can be counted toward the degree each quarter;

  • By the date all grades for the quarter are due, passes at least 8 units each quarter;

  • Pays full tuition to the law school; and,

  • Does not work more than 20 hours per week during the term. (See section entitled ‘Limitations on Working’ for more information.)

A student must be in residence during the quarter in which the final degree is conferred or during the quarter immediately preceding degree conferral.

Faculty Adviser

Each MLS candidate is to have as an adviser a member of the Law School faculty. The faculty adviser shall review for approval the student’s course program and provide general guidance to the student on work at the Law School.

Time Limit on Degree Conferral

Candidates for the MLS degree are expected to complete all degree requirements within one academic year and must complete the degree requirements within two consecutive academic years.

rows.catalogDescription: Through the completion of advanced coursework and strong methodological and analytical training, you’ll prepare to make original contributions to knowledge in linguistics, articulate the results of your work, and demonstrate its significance to linguistics and related fields.

customFields.A3i6E:
Through the completion of advanced coursework and strong methodological and analytical training, the doctoral program prepares students to make original contributions to knowledge in linguistics, articulate the results of their work, and demonstrate its significance to linguistics and related fields. At every stage in the program, students are encouraged to present and publish their research and to develop active professional profiles. 

This program is full time. Students in the doctoral program are expected to maintain a significant physical presence on campus throughout their graduate studies. This ensures that students have access to advisors and mentors, research facilities, libraries, and other resources that support timely progress towards completion of degree requirements. Additionally, being on campus ensures that students are part of the academic and campus community which supports their continued professional development.
customFields.WOZxr: Students who completed graduate coursework at another institution may transfer course units no earlier than the winter quarter of their first year of doctoral study. The Director of Graduate Studies (DGS) evaluates the transfer of units on a course-by-course basis. Students interested in transferring credit should discuss this with the DGS to understand how the transfer of credit will interact with the Linguistics doctoral program; graduate work accepted for transfer of residency does not automatically exempt a student from having to complete a course requirement for the degree.
customFields.ItCSB: The PhD is conferred upon candidates who have demonstrated substantial scholarship and the ability to conduct independent research and analysis in linguistics. By completing advanced coursework and rigorous skills training, students in the doctoral program prepare to make original contributions to linguistic knowledge and to interpret and present the results of such research.

customFields.advisingExpectations:
The department is committed to providing academic advising supporting each graduate student’s scholarly and professional development. The advising relationship should entail collaborative engagement between the advisor and the advisee. Faculty advisors guide students in critical areas such as selecting courses, designing and conducting research, navigating degree requirements, exploring academic and professional opportunities, and preparing for their post-PhD careers. Graduate students are active contributors to the advising relationship, proactively seeking academic and professional guidance and taking responsibility for informing themselves of policies and degree requirements for the doctoral program. An essential part of the advisee-adviser relationship is that students learn to advocate for themselves; this includes discussing expectations for the advisor-advisee relationship with the advisor and revisiting these expectations periodically to ensure mutual understanding.

Advisors and Advising Meetings

A department faculty member is the Director of Graduate Studies (DGS). Typically, the DGS keeps track of the general degree progress of all doctoral students, offers advice on meeting department and university milestones, coordinates departmental advising and TA assignments, and approves special petitions. Each student also has an individual advisor, usually chosen based on shared research interests, who advises on coursework, training in research methodologies, research projects, and professional development. Students are expected to meet regularly with their advisor; in addition, twice a year these meetings take the form of a holistic, structured discussion of the student's recent progress, short-term plans, and longer-term academic and professional goals. Additional details on advising can be found in the Department of Linguistics PhD Handbook.

Additional resources

The Department of Linguistics PhD Handbook provides additional information on advising expectations in the program.

rules.name: Course Requirements Overview
rules.notes: Students should review the Department of Linguistics PhD Handbook for further information regarding the following requirements.
rules.description:
During the first year, doctoral students are expected to take 15 units each quarter of the academic year. Beginning in the second year, students are expected to take 10 units each quarter of the academic year until they reach TGR status. Summer quarter enrollment is determined by the summer activities the student will be engaged in, as well as by the number of units required to ensure timely progress to TGR status.

Doctoral students are required to take nine basic courses. This requirement is designed to guarantee that each student becomes familiar with a range of subfields in linguistics. The basic courses are divided into Groups I, II, and III, and Groups I and II are divided into sets representing subfields. To ensure that students achieve breadth across subfields, there is a cap on the number of courses in any subfield that can be counted towards the basic course requirement; however, students may take more courses in any subfield as additional courses.

The nine basic courses should meet the following criteria:

a. One two course set from Group I.

b. One two course set from Group II.

c. One additional two course set from either Group I or Group II.

d. One additional course from the group with only one set; it should not be from a set used to fulfill items (a)-(c).

e. One course from Group III.

f. One more course from any group; it should not be from a set used to fulfill items (a)-(c).

g. 7 of the 9 basic courses, including two of the three Group I/II sets, must be taken prior to candidacy.

h. All nine basic courses must be taken for a letter grade and completed with a grade of B or better to fulfill the basic course requirement.  Most of these courses should be taken for 4 units; no course may be taken for less than 2 units.
